stem: A development team is deploying an application on EC2 instances that needs to call other AWS services such as S3 and DynamoDB. Which approach is the AWS-recommended way to grant this access?

choices.text: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance profile
Store an IAM user's access key and secret key in the application's configuration file
Hardcode the credentials in the application source code
Use the AWS account's root credentials

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An IAM role attached through an instance profile provides automatically rotated temporary credentials, with no keys stored in the application.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access keys in config: long-term secrets.
• Hardcoded credentials: worst practice.
• Root credentials: never.

Key takeaway: EC2 → AWS APIs = instance profile role.

stem: A company uses AWS Certificate Manager to issue a public certificate for its Application Load Balancer and wants to avoid manual certificate renewal and the risk of an expired certificate causing an outage. What should they do?

choices.text: Use an ACM-issued certificate, which ACM renews automatically
Track the expiration date manually and re-issue the certificate each year
Switch to a self-signed certificate to avoid renewal entirely
Export the certificate and install it on each server behind the ALB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM-issued public certificates used with integrated services such as ALB renew automatically (with DNS validation in place).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual tracking: the error to avoid.
• Self-signed: browsers don't trust it.
• Exporting to servers: public ACM certificates can't be exported.

Key takeaway: ALB TLS without renewals → ACM.

stem: Account A wants to allow a role in Account B to decrypt objects encrypted with a customer managed KMS key owned by Account A. The role in Account B has an IAM policy allowing kms:Decrypt, but decryption still fails. What additional configuration is most likely missing?

choices.text: The S3 bucket policy must allow kms:Decrypt for the Account B role
KMS keys can never be shared across accounts
Account B needs a Direct Connect connection to Account A
The key policy must allow the external account or role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The key policy in Account A must allow the external account or role (and Account B's IAM must also allow kms:Decrypt).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket policy grants KMS: KMS permissions come from key policies.
• Keys can't be shared: they can.
• Direct Connect: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: cross-account KMS → key policy.

stem: A product catalog in RDS MySQL is read thousands of times per second and changes a few times per hour. Stale data up to 5 minutes is acceptable. Which design cuts read load MOST?

choices.text: CloudFront in front of the RDS endpoint
A larger RDS instance class with more memory
ElastiCache cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL
Global Accelerator in front of the application

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A cache-aside layer in ElastiCache serves repeated reads from memory, and a TTL bounds staleness to the acceptable 5 minutes, sharply reducing database queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront: caches HTTP responses at edges; it can't sit in front of a database connection.
• Bigger instance: more capacity, but every read still hits the database.
• Global Accelerator: improves network paths, not database load.

Key takeaway: hot, rarely changing reads with tolerable staleness → cache with a TTL.

stem: A distributed application spans API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB, and the team needs to trace individual requests end-to-end to identify which component is causing intermittent latency. Which service should they use?

choices.text: AWS X-Ray
AWS Config
Amazon Inspector
Amazon CloudWatch Logs alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
X-Ray traces requests across API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB to show where time is spent.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Logs alone: no end-to-end request view.

Key takeaway: end-to-end request tracing → X-Ray.

stem: A gaming application backed by DynamoDB requires microsecond read latency for frequently accessed leaderboard data, faster than what DynamoDB alone typically provides. Which service should be added to the architecture?

choices.text: Amazon RDS Proxy
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
DynamoDB Streams
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, replacing DynamoDB entirely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DAX caches DynamoDB reads in memory for microsecond latency with a DynamoDB-compatible API.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS Proxy: relational connection pooling.
• Streams: change capture.
• Replacing DynamoDB with Redis: a redesign.

Key takeaway: microsecond DynamoDB reads → DAX.

stem: An application deployed behind an Application Load Balancer intermittently loses users' shopping cart contents after requests are routed to a different EC2 instance than the one that started the session. What is the MOST scalable fix?

choices.text: Enable sticky sessions on the ALB and increase the instance count
Switch to a Network Load Balancer to keep source IP affinity
Reduce the ALB idle timeout
Keep cart state in DynamoDB or ElastiCache

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Storing cart state in DynamoDB or ElastiCache makes instances stateless, so any instance can serve any request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sticky sessions: carts lost when instances fail.
• NLB: doesn't fix state.
• Lower idle timeout: unrelated.

Key takeaway: externalize session state.

stem: A mobile app needs to let users submit large video files for processing, such as transcoding and thumbnail generation, that can take several minutes. The client should receive an immediate acknowledgment rather than waiting for processing to complete. Which pattern should the developer implement?

choices.text: A WebSocket connection that blocks until the video finishes processing
Raise the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes and call the function synchronously
Accept the upload, return a request ID, and process asynchronously
A synchronous API Gateway-to-Lambda call that waits for transcoding to finish

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Long-running work shouldn't block the request. Accept the upload, return a request ID, and process asynchronously, letting the client poll or receive a notification.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blocking WebSocket: still waits.
• 15-minute synchronous Lambda: exceeds API limits.
• Synchronous API call: times out.

Key takeaway: long jobs → asynchronous request/response.

stem: A REST API integrated with API Gateway and Lambda begins returning 504 Gateway Timeout errors for a subset of requests that perform a slow third-party lookup. What is the underlying cause?

choices.text: The function's reserved concurrency is set too high for the workload
The function's memory allocation is too high, slowing startup
DynamoDB throttling inside the function is causing the timeout
The backend call exceeds API Gateway's 29-second integration timeout

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway REST integrations time out at 29 seconds by default. A slower backend call returns 504.

Why the other options are wrong:
• High reserved concurrency: doesn't slow calls.
• High memory: speeds startup.
• DynamoDB throttling: would show errors, possibly, but the timeout is the gateway limit.

Key takeaway: 504 from API Gateway → integration timeout.

stem: A Lambda function calls a partner API that returns 429 and 503 errors during bursts. 500 concurrent invocations retry immediately, making things worse, and the function must finish within 10 seconds. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: A fixed 2-second sleep between retries for all concurrent invocations
Immediate retries with the attempt count raised to 10 for every invocation
Capped exponential backoff with jitter, limited attempts within the timeout
Raise the function timeout to 15 minutes so retries always eventually succeed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Backoff spreads retries over time, jitter desynchronizes the 500 callers, and capping delay and attempts keeps total time within the 10-second budget.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Immediate retries: amplify load on a struggling dependency.
• Fixed sleep: callers still retry in synchronized waves.
• 15-minute timeout: breaks the 10-second requirement and ties up concurrency.

Key takeaway: retry budget = backoff + jitter + caps that fit the latency target.

stem: A team is building a public REST API on Amazon API Gateway and needs to release a breaking change to the request schema without disrupting existing client integrations. What is the recommended approach?

choices.text: Overwrite the existing stage in place with the new schema
Publish a new version or stage (v2) and keep v1 running
Delete the old API and publish the new one under the same endpoint
Change only the Lambda code while keeping the same API resource

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Publishing v2 as a new version or stage while keeping v1 running avoids breaking existing clients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overwrite in place: breaks clients.
• Delete old API: breaks clients.
• Change only Lambda: still breaking.

Key takeaway: breaking changes → versioned APIs.

stem: A developer wants to unit test business logic inside a Lambda function handler without deploying to AWS or incurring AWS costs, mocking calls to DynamoDB and S3. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Increase the function timeout
A local test framework with mocked AWS SDK calls
Deploy to a dedicated test account and invoke the function manually
Use X-Ray tracing in production to validate the business logic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Unit tests with a local test framework and mocked AWS SDK calls test business logic quickly without deploying.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Timeout: unrelated.
• Deploy and invoke manually: slow, not unit tests.
• X-Ray in production: not testing.

Key takeaway: unit tests → mocks.

stem: An order processing system requires that messages be processed in the exact order they were sent and that no order is ever processed twice, even at the cost of lower maximum throughput than a standard queue. Which SQS configuration satisfies these requirements?

choices.text: FIFO queue with a maximum message retention period of 14 days
FIFO queue with content-based deduplication enabled
Standard queue with a short visibility timeout
Standard queue with a dead-letter queue configured

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A FIFO queue preserves order, and content-based deduplication prevents duplicates within the 5-minute window.

Why the other options are wrong:
• FIFO with 14-day retention: retention doesn't deduplicate.
• Standard with short timeout: no ordering.
• Standard with DLQ: no ordering.

Key takeaway: ordered and deduplicated → FIFO + deduplication.

stem: A Java application using the AWS SDK experiences intermittent throttling exceptions when calling DynamoDB during traffic spikes. Without changing application logic, which SDK capability should the developer rely on to automatically handle these transient errors?

choices.text: Disabling SSL certificate validation on SDK clients
Polling CloudWatch Logs synchronously before every call
Catching every exception and terminating the process
The SDK's built-in retries with exponential backoff

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The SDK's built-in retries with exponential backoff handle transient throttling automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable SSL validation: insecure.
• Poll CloudWatch Logs: unrelated.
• Terminate on exceptions: not resilient.

Key takeaway: throttling → retries with backoff.

stem: A company needs to ingest clickstream data from millions of website visitors, allow multiple independent applications to consume and replay the same data within a 24-hour window, and process records in order per partition key. Which service BEST fits these requirements over standard SQS?

choices.text: Amazon SQS Standard queue
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon SNS
Amazon SQS FIFO queue

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis Data Streams ingests at high scale and lets multiple independent consumers read the same data, with replay.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS Standard: each message consumed once.
• SNS: no storage or replay.
• SQS FIFO: throughput limits and single consumption.

Key takeaway: multiple consumers + replay → Kinesis.

stem: A Kinesis Data Stream configured with four shards is experiencing ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors during peak write traffic, even though total application throughput requirements have not changed. Records are written using a partition key derived from a customer ID, and a small number of VIP customers generate most of the traffic. What is the MOST likely root cause?

choices.text: Skewed partition keys are creating a hot shard
The stream's retention period is set too low for the data volume
The consuming application is using enhanced fan-out
The shard count exceeds the account's default Kinesis limit

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Throughput exceptions with spare total capacity point to skewed partition keys creating a hot shard. Use higher-cardinality keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Retention: unrelated.
• Enhanced fan-out: consumer side.
• Shard count limit: not the error.

Key takeaway: hot shards → better partition keys.

stem: A developer needs to upgrade a Java 8 service to Java 17, generate unit tests for it, and ask questions about the AWS SDK, all inside VS Code. Which tool fits?

choices.text: The Amazon Bedrock console playground with pasted code
Amazon Q Developer in the IDE
AWS Cloud9 with no AI assistant enabled
Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer comments on pull requests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Q Developer integrates with IDEs such as VS Code, offering code transformation (including Java upgrades), unit test generation, explanations, and AWS guidance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeGuru Reviewer: reviews PRs; no transformation or test generation in the IDE.
• Cloud9 without AI: just an editor.
• Bedrock playground: no IDE or project integration.

Key takeaway: IDE-native AI for transform, test, and explain → Q Developer.

stem: A developer wants an EventBridge rule to trigger a Lambda function only when an S3 object-created event occurs in a specific bucket and the object key ends with .csv. How should this be implemented?

choices.text: Configure S3 to emit events only for .csv files
Write two Lambda functions and let both process every event
An event pattern matching the bucket and a .csv key suffix
CloudWatch alarms with a metric filter on the bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge event pattern can match the bucket name and a key suffix of .csv, so the rule fires only for CSV objects.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 emits only .csv: filtering belongs in the rule.
• Two functions: wasteful.
• CloudWatch alarms: not event routing.

Key takeaway: filter events with patterns.

stem: A team is routing events from over a dozen internal microservices to various targets based on event content, and wants built-in schema discovery plus the ability to route to many AWS service targets, such as Step Functions, Lambda, Kinesis, and API destinations, using content-based filtering rules. Which service better fits these needs?

choices.text: EventBridge (schema registry, many targets, rich patterns)
Amazon SQS, because it guarantees message ordering
Amazon SNS, because it supports message filtering policies
AWS Direct Connect, because it provides private connectivity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge offers content-based routing rules to many targets and a schema registry for event discovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS ordering: not routing.
• SNS filtering: fewer targets and no schema registry.
• Direct Connect: networking.

Key takeaway: event routing → EventBridge.

stem: A microservice repeatedly calls a failing third-party payment API, and each failed call still takes 10 seconds to time out, causing cascading slowdowns and connection pool exhaustion in the calling service. Which pattern should be implemented to prevent this cascading failure?

choices.text: Increase the timeout to 30 seconds so more calls can complete
Increase the number of retry attempts for each failed call
Remove error handling so failures reach the client immediately
A circuit breaker that fails fast after a failure threshold

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A circuit breaker fails fast after repeated failures, preventing threads from waiting on timeouts, and retries later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeout: worse.
• More retries: worse.
• Removing error handling: breaks behavior.

Key takeaway: failing dependency → circuit breaker.

stem: A VPC-attached Lambda function must query RDS in private subnets and also call the public Stripe API. It currently reaches RDS but times out calling Stripe. What fixes this?

choices.text: Assign the Lambda function a public IP address in a public subnet
Add an internet gateway route to the function's private subnets
Remove the function from the VPC so it can reach both services
Route the function's private subnets to a NAT gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC-attached Lambda ENIs have private IPs only. Internet access requires the function's subnets to route through a NAT gateway (in a public subnet), while RDS remains reachable privately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IP: Lambda ENIs don't get public IPs, even in public subnets.
• IGW route from private subnets: doesn't work without public IPs.
• Leaving the VPC: loses private access to RDS.

Key takeaway: VPC Lambda + internet = NAT gateway.

stem: After configuring a Lambda function to run inside a VPC to reach a private ElastiCache cluster, the function now times out on every invocation, including calls to public AWS APIs like DynamoDB that previously worked. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The function's memory is too low to open outbound connections
The ElastiCache cluster's security group is misconfigured
No route to a NAT gateway or VPC endpoint from the subnets
The execution role is missing DynamoDB permissions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A VPC-attached Lambda uses private IPs. Without a route to a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints, it can't reach public AWS services like DynamoDB.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Low memory: unrelated.
• ElastiCache SG: affects ElastiCache, not other services.
• Missing DynamoDB permissions: would show AccessDenied.

Key takeaway: VPC Lambda needs NAT or endpoints.

stem: A Lambda function that processes payment webhooks must never consume more than 20 concurrent executions, regardless of how much traffic other functions in the account receive, to protect a downstream database from overload. What should the developer configure?

choices.text: Provisioned concurrency of 20
A CloudWatch alarm that stops the function after 20 invocations
Reserved concurrency of 20 on that function
An SQS visibility timeout of 20 seconds

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reserved concurrency of 20 caps the function's concurrent executions at 20.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned concurrency: pre-warms, doesn't cap.
• Alarm after 20 invocations: not concurrency.
• Visibility timeout: SQS setting.

Key takeaway: cap concurrency → reserved concurrency.

stem: A latency-sensitive API backed by Lambda experiences unacceptable cold-start latency during sudden traffic spikes at a predictable time each morning. Which Lambda feature directly addresses cold-start latency?

choices.text: Increasing the function's timeout value
Enabling X-Ray active tracing on the function
Provisioned concurrency
Reserved concurrency for the function

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized, avoiding cold starts during traffic spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Timeout: unrelated.
• X-Ray: observation.
• Reserved concurrency: caps, doesn't warm.

Key takeaway: cold starts → provisioned concurrency.

stem: A company wants to capture and forward Lambda telemetry and logs to a third-party observability platform with minimal changes to function code, and needs the forwarding process to run both during and briefly after function invocations complete. Which Lambda feature is designed for this?

choices.text: Increasing the function's memory allocation
A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter
A Lambda extension
A Lambda layer containing only a logging SDK

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Lambda extension runs alongside the function and can capture telemetry and logs and forward them to third-party platforms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More memory: unrelated.
• Subscription filter: works but adds a separate pipeline; extensions integrate directly.
• Layer with SDK only: no lifecycle integration.

Key takeaway: telemetry agents → Lambda extensions.

stem: Uploads to a bucket must trigger two independent consumers: a Lambda thumbnailer for .jpg files only, and an audit pipeline for all objects, each able to fail without affecting the other. Which design fits?

choices.text: One S3 notification to Lambda that calls the audit pipeline
Send S3 events to EventBridge; one rule per consumer
A scheduled Lambda that lists new objects every minute
Two S3 notifications with overlapping prefix and suffix filters

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With EventBridge, S3 events can be filtered by suffix and delivered to multiple independent targets, each with its own retries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Chained Lambda: couples the consumers, so one failure affects both.
• Polling: adds delay and cost.
• Overlapping notification filters: S3 rejects overlapping filters for the same event type.

Key takeaway: fan-out and filtering of S3 events → EventBridge.

stem: Which of the following event sources use Lambda's poll-based event source mapping model, where Lambda itself polls the source and manages batching, rather than the source pushing events directly to Lambda?

choices.text: Amazon SNS and Amazon S3
Amazon EventBridge and AWS Step Functions
Amazon SQS and Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon API Gateway and Application Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SQS and Kinesis use event source mappings where Lambda polls the source.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS and S3: push.
• EventBridge and Step Functions: push/invoke.
• API Gateway and ALB: synchronous invoke.

Key takeaway: poll-based sources → SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams.

stem: An SNS-invoked Lambda function sometimes throws on malformed messages. The team wants failed events kept with error details, and wants to stop after 1 retry instead of the default. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Switch the trigger to synchronous invocation
Wrap the handler in try/catch and swallow all errors
Configure a DLQ on the function with default retries
Max retries 1 plus an on-failure destination

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For asynchronous invocations, Lambda retries twice by default. The asynchronous configuration can reduce retries and set an on-failure destination, which records the event plus error details (richer than a DLQ).

Why the other options are wrong:
• DLQ with defaults: keeps 2 retries, and the DLQ stores only the event.
• Swallowing errors: loses failures silently.
• Synchronous: SNS invokes Lambda asynchronously.

Key takeaway: async failures → tune retries + on-failure destination.

stem: A team wants to capture detailed metadata, including the original event, response payload, and error details, whenever an asynchronous Lambda invocation fails, and route it to an EventBridge event bus for automated remediation workflows. Which feature should they configure?

choices.text: X-Ray tracing with sampling enabled on the function
An on-failure destination to an EventBridge bus
An SQS standard queue configured as a DLQ only
A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter on the function

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An on-failure destination (such as an EventBridge bus) receives the original event, response, and error details for async invocations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: traces.
• DLQ: event only, fewer details.
• Subscription filter: logs.

Key takeaway: failure context → on-failure destinations.

stem: A developer wants to test a Lambda function locally, simulating the Lambda execution environment and invoking it with sample event payloads, before deploying to AWS. Which AWS tool supports this?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail
AWS Config
CloudWatch Synthetics
AWS SAM CLI (sam local invoke)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAM CLI (sam local invoke) runs the function in a Lambda-like container locally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail, Config, Synthetics: not local testing.

Key takeaway: local Lambda testing → SAM CLI.

stem: A developer wants to test a deployed function with a sample SQS batch payload repeatedly, and share the same test event with teammates, without writing code. Which feature fits?

choices.text: AWS Config rules evaluating the function's settings
X-Ray traces from previous invocations
Shareable test events in the Lambda console
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries on the function

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Lambda console Test tab runs a function with a saved JSON event, including templates for services such as SQS. Shareable test events let teammates reuse them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights: analyzes logs; doesn't invoke.
• Config: evaluates configuration.
• X-Ray: observes past invocations; doesn't invoke.

Key takeaway: quick manual invokes → console test events.

stem: A company wants a Lambda function to automatically process every item change in a DynamoDB table, insert, update, or delete, in near real time and in the order changes occurred per partition key. Which integration should be configured?

choices.text: A CloudWatch alarm on DynamoDB consumed capacity
Have the function scan the table every minute for changes
DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda event source mapping
S3 event notifications on the table's backup location

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda event source mapping processes every item change in order per item.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Capacity alarms: not changes.
• Scanning every minute: costly and misses intermediate states.
• S3 backups: unrelated.

Key takeaway: react to table changes → Streams.

stem: A Lambda function experiences long cold starts because it initializes a large SDK client and loads reference data on every cold start, even though this initialization does not change between invocations. What is the recommended optimization?

choices.text: Disable the function's execution role during initialization
Move client and static-data initialization outside the handler
Increase the timeout to absorb slow initialization on every call
Decrease the function's memory allocation to reduce cost

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Initializing clients and static data outside the handler runs once per execution environment and is reused across invocations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable role: nonsense.
• Longer timeout: doesn't speed startup.
• Less memory: slower.

Key takeaway: reuse initialization outside the handler.

stem: A company needs to process IoT sensor data in real time, applying transformations and triggering Lambda functions for anomaly detection within seconds of data arrival, while retaining raw records for up to seven days for reprocessing. Which architecture is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Kinesis Data Streams with extended retention and a Lambda consumer
Write data to S3 and run a nightly AWS Glue ETL job
Store sensor data directly in S3 Glacier for archival
Use Amazon SNS as the only ingestion and storage layer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda consumer processes sensor data in real time, and extended retention allows replay.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly Glue: not real time.
• Glacier: archive.
• SNS only: no storage or replay.

Key takeaway: real-time stream processing → Kinesis + Lambda.

stem: A DynamoDB table storing daily transaction logs uses the transaction date, such as 2026-09-15, as the partition key. During peak hours, the table experiences frequent ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors even though the table's overall provisioned capacity has headroom. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The AWS Region has insufficient DynamoDB capacity for the table
DynamoDB Streams is not enabled, so writes are not distributed
The table's sort key is missing
A day's writes hit one partition key value (hot partition)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Using the date as partition key sends a whole day's writes to one key value, creating a hot partition.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Region capacity: not the cause.
• Streams: unrelated.
• Missing sort key: not the cause.

Key takeaway: low-cardinality partition keys create hot spots.

stem: A checkout reads an item right after writing it and sometimes sees the old value. The read uses GetItem on the base table. What change guarantees the latest value, and what does it cost?

choices.text: Read from a GSI, which is always strongly consistent
ConsistentRead=true; uses twice the read capacity
Enable DynamoDB Streams to force consistency
Use a Scan, which returns the newest version

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GetItem is eventually consistent by default. Setting ConsistentRead=true returns the latest committed value from the base table and consumes twice the read capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GSI: supports only eventually consistent reads.
• Scan: also eventually consistent by default, and expensive.
• Streams: capture changes; they don't change read consistency.

Key takeaway: strong reads = base table + ConsistentRead, at 2× RCU.

stem: A financial application must always read the absolute latest committed value of an account balance immediately after an update, and can tolerate the higher read capacity cost. Which DynamoDB read configuration should be used?

choices.text: An eventually consistent read on the base table
Any read on a global secondary index
A strongly consistent read (ConsistentRead=true)
A Scan operation with a filter expression

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A strongly consistent read (ConsistentRead=true) on the base table returns the latest committed value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Eventually consistent: may be stale.
• GSI reads: eventually consistent.
• Scan: not the point and costly.

Key takeaway: latest value → strongly consistent reads.

stem: A developer attempts to configure a strongly consistent Query against a DynamoDB Global Secondary Index and finds this option is not available. Why?

choices.text: GSIs require ConsistentRead to be false for cost reasons
LSIs have replaced the need for consistent GSI reads
GSIs are updated asynchronously, so reads are eventually consistent
Strongly consistent reads are deprecated in DynamoDB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GSIs are updated asynchronously, so they support only eventually consistent reads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost reasons: not why.
• LSIs replaced: no.
• Deprecated: no.

Key takeaway: GSI reads are eventually consistent.

stem: An Orders table uses partition key customerId and sort key orderDate. A report needs all orders from last month across all customers, run hourly, and the current Scan is expensive. Which fix fits?

choices.text: Strongly consistent Scan reads
A Query using only a filter on orderDate
A parallel Scan with more segments and a filter on orderDate
A GSI keyed on order month with orderDate sort; Query it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Query needs a partition key value. A GSI keyed by month (for example, 'YYYY-MM') lets the report query one partition with a sort key range instead of reading the whole table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Query without a partition key: not possible.
• Parallel Scan: faster, but still reads and pays for every item.
• Consistent Scan: costs more and still reads everything.

Key takeaway: design keys (or GSIs) for the access pattern; avoid Scans for regular reports.

stem: An application performs a DynamoDB Scan with a FilterExpression to find items matching a specific attribute value, and the operation consumes far more read capacity than expected while returning few matching items. What is the root cause and best fix?

choices.text: Filters apply after items are read and charged; use Query/GSI
The FilterExpression syntax is invalid, so the whole table is scanned
The table needs more provisioned write capacity
Scan doesn't support FilterExpression, so this can't occur

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Filters apply after items are read, so a Scan still consumes capacity for every item scanned. Use Query with a key or a GSI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Invalid syntax: no.
• More write capacity: unrelated.
• Scan doesn't support filters: it does.

Key takeaway: filters don't reduce read cost.

stem: A table stores customer orders with CustomerId as the partition key and OrderDate as the sort key. An application needs to retrieve all orders for a single customer placed within the last 30 days, sorted by date. Which operation and key condition should be used?

choices.text: Query on CustomerId with OrderDate BETWEEN the dates
A BatchGetItem call using only the partition key
A Scan of the whole table filtering on CustomerId and OrderDate
A GetItem call for each date in the last 30 days

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Query on CustomerId with OrderDate BETWEEN the two dates reads only the matching items, sorted.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BatchGetItem with only partition key: needs full keys.
• Scan with filter: reads everything.
• GetItem per date: many calls and needs exact keys.

Key takeaway: key-based ranges → Query.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a DynamoDB Global Secondary Index from a Local Secondary Index?

choices.text: An LSI supports only eventually consistent reads; a GSI supports strong reads
A GSI shares the table's throughput; an LSI has its own throughput
No difference; GSI and LSI are two names for the same feature
GSI: any key, created anytime; LSI: same partition key, at creation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A GSI can use any attributes as keys and can be added anytime. An LSI must share the table's partition key and be created with the table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Consistency swapped: LSIs support strong consistency.
• Throughput swapped: GSIs have their own capacity.
• Same feature: different.

Key takeaway: GSI = flexible; LSI = same partition key, at creation.

stem: A table stores chat messages. The app must fetch the latest 20 messages in a room, newest first, efficiently. Which key design fits?

choices.text: Partition key messageId only, then Scan and sort in code
Partition key roomId, sort key timestamp; Query descending, limit 20
Partition key roomId only, with the timestamp as a regular attribute
Partition key timestamp, sort key roomId

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A composite key groups items by roomId and orders them by timestamp. A Query with ScanIndexForward=false and Limit=20 returns the newest messages efficiently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• messageId + Scan: reads the whole table.
• Timestamp partition: scatters a room's messages and creates hot keys.
• roomId only: one item per room, since keys must be unique.

Key takeaway: partition = the group you query by; sort = the order you need.

stem: A DynamoDB table stores millions of orders, and only a small percentage have a Status attribute set to RETURNED. An application needs to efficiently query only the returned orders without scanning the full table. Which design technique is MOST efficient?

choices.text: Store returned orders in a separate S3 bucket instead of DynamoDB
A sparse GSI keyed on Status
Add Status as a sort key on the table's existing primary key
Run a scheduled Scan with a FilterExpression on Status = RETURNED

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A sparse GSI keyed on Status contains only items that have the attribute, so querying returned orders reads a small index.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate S3 store: complicates data.
• Status as sort key: changes the primary key.
• Scheduled Scan: costly.

Key takeaway: find a small subset → sparse index.

stem: A developer's DynamoDB code is full of type descriptors like {"S": ...} and {"N": ...} and bugs from converting numbers. Which change reduces this boilerplate?

choices.text: Use the SDK's document client or object mapper
Store every attribute as a string to avoid types
Use BatchWriteItem for all writes
Switch to PartiQL so types are no longer needed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Document clients and object mappers (such as the AWS SDK Enhanced Client or DynamoDB Document Client) convert native types to and from DynamoDB's attribute-value format automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All strings: loses numeric sorting and arithmetic.
• PartiQL: still returns typed attribute values from the low-level API.
• BatchWriteItem: about batching, not types.

Key takeaway: let the higher-level client handle marshalling.

stem: A Lambda function using the low-level DynamoDB API attempts to write an item and receives a validation error because a numeric application value was passed as a plain JSON number rather than being wrapped correctly for DynamoDB's attribute format. What is the correct way to represent a numeric attribute using the DynamoDB low-level API JSON format?

choices.text: 42 as a bare JSON value with no type wrapper
{"Number": 42}

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The low-level API wraps each value with a type descriptor. Numbers use N with the value as a string: {"N": "42"}.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bare value: missing type.
• S type: string, not number.
• Number key: invalid descriptor.

Key takeaway: low-level DynamoDB types need descriptors.

stem: A DynamoDB table stores session tokens that should be automatically deleted 24 hours after creation without consuming write capacity for the deletion or requiring a scheduled job. Which DynamoDB feature should be used?

choices.text: DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL) attribute
Switching the table's billing mode to on-demand
A scheduled Lambda function that scans and deletes expired items hourly
Enabling DynamoDB Streams only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A TTL attribute with an expiration timestamp lets DynamoDB delete items automatically at no write cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand: billing mode.
• Scheduled scan and delete: costly.
• Streams only: no deletion.

Key takeaway: automatic expiry → TTL.

stem: A team needs the ability to restore a DynamoDB table to any point in time within the last 35 days in case of accidental data corruption. Which feature should be enabled?

choices.text: DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery
Global Tables
DynamoDB Streams
On-demand backups only, taken manually once a month

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Point-in-time recovery restores a table to any second within the last 35 days.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Global Tables: replication.
• Streams: change capture.
• Monthly on-demand backups: coarse.

Key takeaway: any point in 35 days → PITR.

stem: A read-heavy web application queries the same set of product catalog data from DynamoDB thousands of times per second, and the team wants to reduce read costs and latency for this repeatedly requested data without changing DynamoDB's schema. Which caching approach is well suited as a general-purpose, flexible in-memory cache sitting in front of the application's data access layer?

choices.text: Switch to provisioned capacity with auto scaling only
Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table
ElastiCache as a cache-aside layer
Increase the table's provisioned write capacity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ElastiCache as a cache-aside layer serves repeated reads from memory, cutting DynamoDB reads and latency (DAX is another option).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Auto scaling: doesn't cut repeated reads.
• Streams: change capture.
• Write capacity: reads are the issue.

Key takeaway: repeated reads → cache.

stem: A product catalog lives in DynamoDB. Users need fuzzy full-text search with relevance ranking and facets. Which design fits?

choices.text: Move the catalog to S3 and query with Athena per request
Scan with contains() filters on each request
Add GSIs for every searchable word
Stream changes into OpenSearch Service and search there

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch provides full-text search, fuzzy matching, relevance scoring, and aggregations (facets). DynamoDB Streams, or the zero-ETL integration, keeps the index in sync while DynamoDB stays the system of record.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scan with contains(): slow, expensive, and no relevance ranking.
• GSIs per word: impractical and not full-text.
• Athena per request: too slow for interactive search.

Key takeaway: full-text search → OpenSearch alongside the primary database.

stem: An application needs to let users perform full-text search with typo tolerance and relevance ranking across millions of product descriptions, a capability that DynamoDB's Query and Scan operations cannot efficiently provide. What is a common architecture pattern to add this capability?

choices.text: Replace DynamoDB entirely with S3 for all storage and searching
Run a Scan with a contains() filter on every request
Increase provisioned read capacity so DynamoDB supports full-text search
Stream changes into OpenSearch and search there

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Streaming changes into OpenSearch provides full-text search with typo tolerance and relevance ranking.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 for all: no search.
• Scan with contains(): slow and no relevance.
• More read capacity: doesn't add search.

Key takeaway: full-text search → OpenSearch.

stem: An OpenSearch Service domain used for log analytics is experiencing degraded query performance and a yellow cluster health status as log volume grows. Which action is MOST likely to address sustained ingestion and query growth?

choices.text: Switch all indices to a single primary shard regardless of data volume
Disable replica shards entirely to free resources
Move all data into one index with no time-based rotation
Add data nodes and revisit the sharding strategy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Adding data nodes and revisiting shard count and size relieves resource pressure and improves query performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single primary shard: limits parallelism.
• No replicas: hurts availability and reads.
• One index with no rotation: grows unbounded.

Key takeaway: OpenSearch performance → capacity + sharding strategy.

stem: A web app needs username and password sign-up, MFA, social login with Google, and JWTs for its API. Which service fits?

choices.text: A Cognito identity pool alone
A Cognito user pool with Google federation and MFA
IAM Identity Center for customers
IAM users created for each customer with console passwords

explanation:
Why this is correct:
User pools are user directories that handle sign-up, sign-in, MFA, and social or SAML federation, and issue JWTs (ID and access tokens) the API can validate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity pools: issue AWS credentials; they aren't a user directory.
• IAM users: not for app end users.
• Identity Center: workforce access to AWS, not customer apps.

Key takeaway: app users and JWTs → user pool; AWS credentials → identity pool.

stem: A mobile application authenticates users through a Cognito User Pool. The app then needs to let authenticated users upload photos directly to an S3 bucket using temporary AWS credentials scoped to each user. What should the developer configure?

choices.text: A Cognito identity pool using the user pool, mapped to an IAM role
A long-lived IAM access key embedded in the mobile app
A Lambda authorizer attached to the S3 bucket policy
An IAM user created for each application user

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Cognito identity pool that trusts the user pool exchanges tokens for temporary credentials mapped to a scoped IAM role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Embedded access key: insecure.
• Lambda authorizer on S3: doesn't exist.
• IAM user per app user: unmanageable.

Key takeaway: app users → AWS credentials via identity pools.

stem: A company wants to let external users authenticate using either an existing SAML 2.0 corporate identity provider or a public OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, and then obtain temporary AWS credentials to call AWS APIs directly, without creating IAM users for each person. Which two AWS federation mechanisms support this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Attaching an S3 bucket policy that allows anonymous access
Creating individual IAM users that mirror each external identity
Web identity federation using OIDC via an IAM OIDC identity provider or Amazon Cognito Identity Pools
Sharing the AWS account root user credentials with external users
SAML 2.0 federation configured as an identity provider in IAM

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAML 2.0 federation supports corporate identity providers, and web identity federation via an IAM OIDC provider supports OIDC providers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Anonymous bucket access: insecure.
• Mirror IAM users: unmanageable.
• Root credentials: never.

Key takeaway: external identities → SAML or OIDC federation.

stem: An API accepts bearer tokens in the Authorization header. A token leaked in a public log. What does this mean, and which mitigation fits BEST?

choices.text: It is safe because tokens are encrypted with KMS
Anyone holding it can use it; shorten expiry, revoke tokens
Nothing, since bearer tokens are bound to the original client's IP
It is unusable without the user's password

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bearer tokens grant access to whoever presents them. Keep access tokens short-lived, revoke refresh tokens (Cognito supports token revocation), and never log tokens.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IP binding: not a property of bearer tokens.
• Password needed: the token itself is the credential.
• KMS encryption: the token is signed, and possession is what matters.

Key takeaway: bearer = possession; minimize lifetime and exposure.

stem: A serverless API secured by Amazon API Gateway uses a Lambda authorizer that validates a JWT bearer token passed in the Authorization header. Clients report receiving 401 Unauthorized responses even though their tokens have not expired. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The stage is not associated with a custom domain name
The function's reserved concurrency is set too high
The token is missing the Bearer prefix or is in the wrong header
The S3 bucket storing the deployment package is versioned

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Lambda authorizer receives the token from the configured header. A missing Bearer prefix or wrong header makes validation fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom domain: unrelated.
• Reserved concurrency: unrelated.
• Versioned bucket: unrelated.

Key takeaway: check the token source and format first.

stem: A developer needs to run AWS CLI commands against two different AWS accounts from the same workstation without repeatedly re-entering credentials. What should they configure?

choices.text: A single IAM user shared between both accounts
Named CLI profiles selected with --profile
A bearer token stored in an environment variable
Two separate installations of the AWS CLI

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Named profiles in the CLI config store separate credentials or role settings, selected with --profile.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared IAM user: poor practice.
• Bearer token: not how the CLI authenticates.
• Two installations: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: multiple accounts in the CLI → named profiles.

stem: A Lambda function's execution role attempts to call sts:AssumeRole on a role in another AWS account, but the call fails with an AccessDenied error. The execution role's policy already grants sts:AssumeRole on the target role's ARN. What else must be verified?

choices.text: That the function has a reserved concurrency limit configured
That the target role's trust policy trusts the caller
That the target role has AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole attached
That the deployment package bucket has server-side encryption enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The target role's trust policy must trust the caller's execution role (and the caller needs sts:AssumeRole permission).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reserved concurrency: unrelated.
• BasicExecutionRole on target: unrelated.
• Bucket encryption: unrelated.

Key takeaway: AssumeRole needs trust.

stem: A build server in another cloud currently uses an IAM user's access keys to deploy to AWS. Security wants no long-term credentials. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Rotate the IAM user's access keys weekly
Create a second IAM user for backup deployments
Store the keys in Secrets Manager on the build server
OIDC federation to an IAM role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Roles have no long-term credentials. Trusting the build system's OIDC provider lets it exchange its identity token for temporary role credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Weekly rotation: still long-term keys.
• Second user: more long-term keys.
• Secrets Manager: stores keys but doesn't make them temporary.

Key takeaway: users hold long-term keys; roles give temporary credentials.

stem: A platform team wants to allow individual developers to create their own IAM roles for their projects, but wants to guarantee that no role a developer creates can ever exceed a fixed maximum set of permissions, regardless of the policies attached to it. Which IAM feature is designed for this?

choices.text: IAM groups
Resource-based policies
Service control policies applied only at the account root
Permissions boundaries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Permissions boundaries let developers create roles while capping the maximum permissions those roles can have.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Groups: users only.
• Resource-based policies: grant access to resources.
• Root SCP only: account-wide, not per role.

Key takeaway: safe delegation → permissions boundaries.

stem: A SaaS application stores each customer's data in a shared Amazon DynamoDB table, using a partition key that includes the customer/tenant ID. The application needs to ensure that each authenticated end user, via temporary credentials obtained through a Cognito Identity Pool, can only access DynamoDB items belonging to their own tenant. Which mechanism enables this at the AWS level?

choices.text: dynamodb:LeadingKeys conditions scoped to the tenant
Turning on point-in-time recovery for the table
A bearer token validated only by the application's own code
Enabling DynamoDB Streams on the table

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An IAM condition on dynamodb:LeadingKeys restricts each tenant's credentials to items with their partition key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• PITR: backups.
• Application-only token validation: no enforcement in AWS.
• Streams: change capture.

Key takeaway: tenant row isolation in DynamoDB → LeadingKeys.

stem: An API must authorize requests using a partner's proprietary HMAC header, and cache decisions for 5 minutes to reduce latency. Which API Gateway feature fits?

choices.text: An API key with a usage plan and throttling per partner
IAM authorization with SigV4
A Cognito user pool authorizer
A Lambda authorizer (request type) with result caching

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda authorizers run custom logic, such as validating a proprietary signature, return an IAM policy, and can cache results by identity source for a TTL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito authorizer: validates Cognito JWTs only.
• IAM SigV4: requires AWS credentials.
• API keys: identify clients for quotas; not authentication.

Key takeaway: custom auth schemes → Lambda authorizer.

stem: In a microservices architecture running on Amazon ECS, Service A needs to invoke an internal API exposed by Service B through Amazon API Gateway, and calls must be authenticated using AWS Signature Version 4 rather than a shared API key. What should be configured?

choices.text: Share Service B's IAM user access keys in Service A's container image
A task role for Service A, IAM auth on the method, SigV4 signing
Disable authorization on the method to simplify communication
A Cognito identity pool unauthenticated role for Service A

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service A's task role signs requests with SigV4, and the API method uses IAM authorization to allow only that role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared keys: insecure.
• No authorization: insecure.
• Unauthenticated Cognito role: not service identity.

Key takeaway: service-to-service auth → IAM auth + SigV4.

stem: A team is deciding how two internal microservices deployed on Amazon EKS should authenticate to each other: mutual TLS (mTLS) via a service mesh, or SigV4-signed requests using IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA). Which statement accurately describes a tradeoff between these approaches?

choices.text: IRSA cannot be used with Amazon EKS clusters
mTLS and IRSA are identical and interchangeable in every scenario
mTLS works at transport level with CA overhead; IRSA/SigV4 uses IAM
mTLS eliminates the need for any certificate management

explanation:
Why this is correct:
mTLS authenticates at the transport level but needs a CA and certificate management. IRSA with SigV4 uses IAM identities for AWS-style authorization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IRSA not on EKS: it's for EKS.
• Identical: different layers.
• mTLS needs no certificates: it does.

Key takeaway: mTLS vs. IAM identity: different tradeoffs.

stem: A role's only policy allows dynamodb:GetItem on table Orders. The function also calls Query on Orders and PutItem on Audit. What happens?

choices.text: Everything is allowed since there's no explicit Deny
All DynamoDB actions are allowed on Orders
Only GetItem on Orders succeeds
GetItem is denied because a Deny is required first

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM denies by default. Only explicitly allowed actions on the listed resources succeed; Query and PutItem have no allow statement, so they're implicitly denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All actions on Orders: GetItem doesn't imply Query.
• No explicit Deny means allow: the default is deny.
• Deny required: allows work without any deny statement.

Key takeaway: default deny; grant each needed action explicitly.

stem: A developer is a member of two IAM groups. One group's policy allows s3:DeleteObject on a bucket, and the other group's policy explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject on the same bucket. When the developer attempts to delete an object in that bucket, what is the result?

choices.text: Denied; an explicit Deny overrides any Allow
It depends on which group was created first
Allowed, because at least one policy grants the permission
Allowed, because group memberships are evaluated independently

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An explicit Deny in any applicable policy overrides any Allow, so the action is denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Group creation order: irrelevant.
• Allowed because one allows: deny wins.
• Independent evaluation: all policies combine.

Key takeaway: explicit deny always wins.

stem: A company must ensure that no clients can access objects in an S3 bucket over unencrypted HTTP. Which approach enforces this requirement?

choices.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration
Enable default encryption with SSE-S3
Enable versioning on the bucket
Deny when aws:SecureTransport is false

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy denying requests when aws:SecureTransport is false blocks HTTP access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• SSE-S3: at rest.
• Versioning: data protection.

Key takeaway: enforce HTTPS → SecureTransport deny.

stem: An application connects to an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance, and the security team requires that all connections use SSL/TLS. Developers report that some client connections still succeed without SSL. What should be done to fully enforce encrypted connections?

choices.text: Enforce SSL with require_secure_transport in the parameter group
Enable RDS storage encryption on the instance
Rotate the RDS master password regularly
Enable a Multi-AZ deployment for the instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Setting require_secure_transport in the DB parameter group forces all MySQL connections to use SSL/TLS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Storage encryption: at rest.
• Password rotation: authentication.
• Multi-AZ: availability.

Key takeaway: enforce TLS on RDS MySQL → parameter group.

stem: Internal microservices on ECS need mutual TLS with certificates trusted only inside the company, issued automatically and rotated frequently. Which service fits?

choices.text: KMS asymmetric keys used as certificates
AWS Private CA issuing short-lived private certificates
ACM public certificates with DNS validation
Self-signed certificates generated by each service and stored in S3

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Private CA issues private certificates for internal names and clients, can issue short-lived certificates, and integrates with services and automation. Public CAs can't issue for private-only names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public ACM: for public domains; not client certificates for internal mTLS.
• Self-signed: no trust chain management or automation.
• KMS keys: keys, not X.509 certificates.

Key takeaway: internal trust → a private CA.

stem: A company is building an internal microservices platform where services communicate over mTLS, and certificates must be issued to hundreds of internal endpoints not exposed to the internet, with full control over the certificate hierarchy. Which service should be used to issue these certificates?

choices.text: Amazon Cognito
The public AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate issuance for internet-facing endpoints
AWS Certificate Manager Private Certificate Authority (ACM Private CA)
AWS Secrets Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM Private CA issues private certificates for internal mTLS between services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito: user auth.
• Public ACM: public names.
• Secrets Manager: secrets storage.

Key takeaway: internal certificates → Private CA.

stem: A company operates a centralized AWS Certificate Manager Private CA in a shared services account and wants application teams in other member accounts within AWS Organizations to be able to request certificates from that same CA without creating a new CA in each account. What AWS feature enables this?

choices.text: AWS RAM sharing of the private CA
Copying the CA's private key into each account
AWS Organizations service control policies
Cross-account S3 bucket policies

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS RAM can share a Private CA with other accounts so they can issue certificates from it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copying the private key: impossible and unsafe.
• SCPs: don't share resources.
• Bucket policies: unrelated.

Key takeaway: share a CA across accounts → RAM.

stem: A company must ensure that AWS never has access to plaintext customer files, even though they are stored in S3. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SSE-C, with the key sent on each request
SSE-S3 default encryption with S3-managed keys on the bucket
Client-side encryption with keys held only by the company
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With client-side encryption, data is encrypted before upload with keys AWS never receives, so S3 stores only ciphertext.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-KMS: S3 decrypts using KMS on authorized reads, so AWS systems handle plaintext.
• SSE-S3: AWS manages the keys.
• SSE-C: the key is sent to S3 on each request, so S3 handles plaintext and key in memory.

Key takeaway: 'AWS must never see plaintext' → client-side encryption.

stem: A financial services company must guarantee that S3 objects containing highly sensitive data are encrypted before they ever leave application servers, and that AWS never has access to the plaintext data or the key used to encrypt it. Which approach should the developer implement?

choices.text: S3 default bucket encryption with an AWS owned key
Client-side encryption with a local key before upload
SSE-KMS using an AWS managed key
SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Client-side encryption with a local key encrypts data before upload, so AWS never sees plaintext.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS owned key: server side.
• SSE-KMS managed key: server side.
• SSE-S3: server side.

Key takeaway: never plaintext in AWS → client-side encryption.

stem: An application needs to encrypt large files locally before uploading them, using AWS KMS to protect the encryption key without sending each large file through the 4 KB request-size-limited Encrypt API. Which KMS pattern should be used?

choices.text: Call KMS Encrypt on the whole file regardless of its size
Disable key rotation to allow larger payloads
Store the KMS key material directly on the client
Envelope encryption with a GenerateDataKey data key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Envelope encryption uses GenerateDataKey to get a data key, encrypts the file locally, and stores the encrypted data key alongside it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encrypt whole file: 4 KB limit.
• Disable rotation: unrelated.
• Store key material locally: not possible with KMS.

Key takeaway: large data → envelope encryption.

stem: Which statement correctly compares key rotation between AWS managed KMS keys and customer managed KMS keys?

choices.text: Both share identical rotation schedules set by the customer
AWS managed keys rotate automatically; CMK rotation is optional
AWS managed keys can never be rotated
Customer managed keys cannot be rotated under any circumstances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS managed keys rotate automatically. Customer managed key rotation is optional and configurable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Customer sets both schedules: no.
• Managed keys never rotate: they do.
• CMKs can't rotate: they can.

Key takeaway: managed = automatic; CMK = optional.

stem: A developer is launching a new Amazon EC2 instance and needs a way to securely connect to it using SSH with key-based authentication instead of a password. What is the correct way to do this using EC2 key pairs?

choices.text: Use the account root user password as the SSH credential
Store the private key in a public S3 bucket for easy access
Specify an EC2 key pair at launch and SSH with its private key
Generate the key pair in KMS and put the private key in user data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Specify an EC2 key pair at launch and connect with its private key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Root password: no.
• Public bucket: exposes key.
• KMS key pair in user data: exposes key.

Key takeaway: SSH access → key pairs.

stem: An auditor asks how data moving between a Lambda function and DynamoDB is protected, and whether traffic can avoid the internet. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: Protected only when the function runs outside a VPC
TLS by default; a gateway endpoint keeps it private
Encrypted only if the table uses a customer managed key
Plaintext unless the client enables TLS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB API endpoints use HTTPS/TLS. For VPC-attached functions, a DynamoDB gateway endpoint keeps traffic on the AWS network instead of going through a NAT gateway to the public endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Plaintext by default: endpoints are HTTPS.
• CMK: at-rest encryption, not transit.
• Outside a VPC: TLS applies either way.

Key takeaway: transit = TLS; private path = VPC endpoint.

stem: After a scheduled maintenance window, client applications start failing to establish HTTPS connections to an internal service secured with a certificate issued by AWS Private CA, reporting an untrusted certificate error, even though the certificate itself has not expired. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The service uses an EC2 key pair instead of a certificate
Clients don't trust the private CA's certificate chain
The private CA's certificate was rotated automatically without customer control
AWS Private CA issued a certificate with a public trust anchor by default

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Certificates from a private CA fail unless clients trust the CA chain. Install the private CA root in clients' trust stores.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 key pair: unrelated.
• Automatic rotation without notice: not the main cause.
• Public trust anchor: private CAs aren't publicly trusted.

Key takeaway: private certs need client trust.

stem: All EBS volumes for a workload must be encrypted with a customer managed key, and a snapshot must be restorable in a DR account. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Enable S3 default encryption on the snapshot bucket
Use the AWS managed aws/ebs key and share the snapshot
Encrypt files in the OS and keep volumes unencrypted
CMK encryption; share snapshot and key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS encryption with a customer managed key covers volumes and snapshots. Sharing an encrypted snapshot requires sharing the snapshot and granting the other account use of the key; the AWS managed key can't be shared.

Why the other options are wrong:
• aws/ebs: snapshots encrypted with it can't be shared cross-account.
• OS-level only: volumes and snapshots stay unencrypted.
• S3 encryption: you don't manage the storage behind EBS snapshots.

Key takeaway: cross-account encrypted snapshots need a shareable CMK.

stem: A team is classifying data fields for a privacy review. Which field is personal data on its own or in combination, and needs protection?

choices.text: The API version number returned in headers
A customer's name with their home address
A server log's timestamp format string
The AWS Region name where a service is deployed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A name combined with an address identifies a person and is personally identifiable information, requiring controls such as encryption, masking, and access limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• API version, Region name, timestamp format: technical metadata that doesn't identify a person.

Key takeaway: PII = data that identifies a person, alone or combined.

stem: A healthcare application processes Protected Health Information (PHI) and must run on AWS in a manner consistent with HIPAA requirements. What must the development team do before storing any PHI in an AWS service?

choices.text: Use only Amazon Cognito for all data storage
Nothing beyond enabling default encryption
A BAA with AWS and only BAA-covered services
Enable versioning on any S3 buckets used

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Processing PHI on AWS requires a Business Associate Addendum with AWS and using only HIPAA-eligible services, plus appropriate configuration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito for storage: nonsense.
• Default encryption only: insufficient.
• Versioning: not compliance.

Key takeaway: PHI → BAA + eligible services.

stem: A function's environment variables hold a third-party API key. Security requires that only the function's role can decrypt it and that decryption is logged. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Rely on the default AWS managed key encryption
Store the key in plaintext and restrict console access
Base64-encode the value before saving it
A CMK whose policy allows only that role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda encrypts environment variables at rest with an AWS managed key by default. Using a customer managed key lets the key policy restrict who can decrypt, and CloudTrail logs KMS usage. For sensitive values, consider encryption helpers or Secrets Manager.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default key: anyone who can view the function configuration can see the values.
• Console restrictions: plaintext is still exposed via APIs.
• Base64: encoding, not encryption.

Key takeaway: control who can decrypt → a customer managed key.

stem: A developer wants to store a database connection string as a Lambda environment variable but requires the ability to control and audit exactly which principals can decrypt that value, separate from Lambda's default behavior. What should the developer do?

choices.text: Store it as plaintext, since environment variables can't use custom keys
Hardcode the value as a string in the function's code
Encrypt the variables with a customer managed KMS key
Disable encryption on the function entirely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda environment variables can be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, controlling who can decrypt them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't use CMKs: they can.
• Hardcode: worse.
• Disable encryption: not allowed and insecure.

Key takeaway: sensitive env vars → CMK encryption.

stem: An app has database credentials hardcoded in source. Which TWO benefits would moving them to Secrets Manager provide? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Scheduled rotation without code changes
IAM-controlled, audited access to each secret
Automatic scaling of the database
Conversion of NoSQL schemas to relational
Free, unlimited API calls

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager controls access with IAM and resource policies, logs retrieval in CloudTrail, and rotates credentials on a schedule using managed or custom Lambda rotation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scaling: unrelated.
• Free API calls: API calls are billed.
• Schema conversion: unrelated.

Key takeaway: secrets out of code → access control, audit, and rotation.

stem: A team needs to decide between AWS Secrets Manager and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to store a database password that must be automatically rotated on a fixed schedule using AWS-provided rotation logic. Which service should they choose and why?

choices.text: Secrets Manager (native rotation templates)
Either service rotates credentials identically out of the box
Secrets Manager cannot store database credentials
Parameter Store, which is always the cheaper option

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager provides native rotation templates for database credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical rotation: Parameter Store lacks it.
• Can't store DB credentials: it can.
• Parameter Store cheaper: but lacks rotation.

Key takeaway: rotating credentials → Secrets Manager.

stem: An ECS task's application code calls the Secrets Manager GetSecretValue API to retrieve a database credential but receives an AccessDeniedException, even though the secret exists and the task role has an attached policy allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret's ARN. The secret is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. What is the MOST likely missing piece?

choices.text: The key policy doesn't allow the task role to use kms:Decrypt
The ECS cluster does not have Container Insights enabled
The task definition does not specify a launch type
The secret's rotation configuration is disabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the secret uses a customer managed key, the task role needs kms:Decrypt through the key policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Container Insights: unrelated.
• Launch type: unrelated.
• Rotation disabled: doesn't block reads.

Key takeaway: secret reads with CMKs need key access.

stem: A security team wants to automatically detect and mask sensitive data patterns, such as Social Security numbers, that might inadvertently appear in existing CloudWatch Logs log groups, without modifying the application code. Which native CloudWatch capability addresses this?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs data protection policies
CloudWatch composite alarms on log metrics
Logs Insights query result caching
Log group encryption with a KMS key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Logs data protection policies detect and mask sensitive data such as SSNs in log events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Composite alarms: alerts.
• Query caching: no.
• KMS encryption: at rest, not masking.

Key takeaway: mask sensitive log data → data protection policies.

stem: A customer support application displays customer records to support agents, but company policy requires that only the last four digits of a customer's Social Security number be visible to agents by default, with full access requiring a separate elevated permission. Where should this masking logic MOST appropriately be enforced?

choices.text: Grant all support agents administrator IAM permissions
Role-based field masking in the application layer
Rely on S3 bucket encryption where the data is stored
Store masked and full SSN copies with no extra access control

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Role-based masking in the application shows full SSNs only to authorized roles and masked values to others.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Admin for all: violates policy.
• Bucket encryption: doesn't mask displays.
• Masked copies without controls: still exposed.

Key takeaway: field-level visibility → app-layer masking.

stem: A multi-tenant SaaS application stores all tenants' data in a single shared Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database and table. The development team wants to ensure a query executed under one tenant's context can never accidentally return another tenant's rows, even if a query is missing a WHERE clause filter due to a bug. Which native PostgreSQL/RDS feature helps enforce this at the database level?

choices.text: Row-level security policies based on tenant context
Automated backups of the database
IAM database authentication alone
A Multi-AZ deployment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
PostgreSQL row-level security policies filter rows by tenant context, isolating tenants in a shared database.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Backups: unrelated.
• IAM DB auth alone: authenticates, doesn't isolate rows.
• Multi-AZ: availability.

Key takeaway: shared-DB tenant isolation → RLS.

stem: A SaaS company is designing tenant data isolation and is weighing a pool model, where all tenants share the same database and tables isolated logically by tenant ID and access controls, against a silo model, where each tenant gets a fully separate database or AWS account. Which statement correctly describes a tradeoff between these models?

choices.text: There is no meaningful difference in isolation strength
The pool model gives automatic per-tenant keys with no extra setup
The silo model always has weaker isolation than the pool model
Pool is cheaper but needs stricter controls; silo isolates best at higher cost

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A pool model is cheaper but needs strict tenant isolation controls. A silo model isolates tenants best at higher cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No difference: silo is stronger.
• Pool gives automatic per-tenant keys: no.
• Silo weaker: no.

Key takeaway: pool vs. silo = cost vs. isolation.

stem: A multi-tenant application wants to ensure that if one tenant's KMS-managed encryption key is ever compromised or disabled, only that tenant's data becomes inaccessible, without affecting other tenants. What design approach supports this?

choices.text: Store all tenants' data with the same static encryption password in application code
Use a single shared AWS managed KMS key for all tenants' data
Disable encryption for all tenants to avoid dependency on any key
Use a separate customer managed KMS key per tenant to encrypt that tenant's data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A separate customer managed KMS key per tenant limits the impact of a compromised key to that tenant.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same password: shared blast radius.
• Shared managed key: shared blast radius.
• No encryption: unacceptable.

Key takeaway: per-tenant keys contain blast radius.

stem: Developers need a copy of production data in staging for realistic testing, but must not see real customer names, emails, or card numbers. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Copy the data as-is and restrict it with IAM
Encrypt staging with the production KMS key
Give developers read access to production instead
Anonymize or tokenize PII in the copy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Masking or tokenizing sensitive fields before the data reaches lower environments removes exposure while keeping data realistic. Tools such as Glue DataBrew or custom ETL can do this.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Production access: exposes real PII.
• Encryption: authorized readers still see plaintext.
• IAM on raw data: developers with access still see PII.

Key takeaway: protect PII by transforming it, not only by restricting it.

stem: One Lambda package runs in dev, test, and prod with different database endpoints. Prod values change occasionally without redeploying. Which TWO approaches fit? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Put the values in the execution role's trust policy
Embed the values in the zip package
Read values from Parameter Store at runtime (with caching)
Hardcode the values in the source code
Set per-environment environment variables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Environment variables separate configuration per function or stage. Parameter Store lets values change without a deployment when read at runtime with sensible caching.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcoding or embedding: require rebuilds per environment.
• Trust policy: defines who can assume the role, not configuration.

Key takeaway: externalize configuration from the artifact.

stem: Running sam build in a subdirectory fails with 'Template file not found'. The template is at infra/app.yaml. What fixes it?

choices.text: Commit the template to CodeCommit first
Use sam build --template-file infra/app.yaml
Rename the template to template.json in any folder
Move the template into .aws-sam/build

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The SAM CLI looks for template.yaml (or template.yml) in the current directory by default. Point it to another location with --template-file (or -t), or run from the directory containing the template.

Why the other options are wrong:
• template.json elsewhere: still not found in the current directory.
• .aws-sam/build: build output, not the source template location.
• CodeCommit: unrelated to local builds.

Key takeaway: SAM defaults to ./template.yaml; override with -t.

stem: A pipeline must start automatically when code is pushed to main in GitHub, but not for pushes to other branches, and without storing a GitHub personal access token. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A developer running StartPipelineExecution manually
A GitHub v1 source action authenticated with a personal access token
A CodeConnections source action on main with a push trigger
An hourly EventBridge schedule starting the pipeline

explanation:
Why this is correct:
