CodeConnections (formerly CodeStar Connections) authorizes CodePipeline to GitHub through an app installation instead of a stored token. The source action watches a branch, and pipeline triggers can filter on branch pushes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GitHub v1 with PAT: stores a token and is a legacy action.
• Hourly schedule: not event-driven.
• Manual start: not automatic.

Key takeaway: GitHub + CodePipeline → CodeConnections.

stem: A team wants to turn on a new pricing feature for 10% of users, then 50%, then all, with automatic rollback if the error alarm fires, without redeploying code. Which service fits?

choices.text: AppConfig flags with gradual rollout and rollback
Parameter Store with a manual update each day
A Lambda alias with weighted routing
A CloudFormation change set

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AppConfig deploys configuration and feature flags gradually according to a deployment strategy, monitors CloudWatch alarms, and rolls back automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store: no staged rollout or automatic rollback.
• Lambda alias: shifts traffic between code versions, not per-user flags.
• Change set: infrastructure changes.

Key takeaway: runtime flags with safe rollout → AppConfig.

stem: A team wants AWS AppConfig to automatically reject a new configuration deployment if the configuration data does not match an expected JSON structure, before it ever reaches an application host. Which AppConfig feature should they use?

choices.text: A CodeBuild buildspec validation phase
A permissions boundary on the AppConfig role
A JSON Schema or Lambda validator on the profile
A CloudWatch alarm on the strategy's bake time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AppConfig validators (a JSON Schema or a Lambda function) on the configuration profile reject invalid configurations before deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeBuild validation: outside AppConfig.
• Permissions boundary: unrelated.
• Bake-time alarm: after deployment starts.

Key takeaway: validate config before deploy → AppConfig validators.

stem: After running sam build in an AWS SAM project, where does the SAM CLI place the built deployment artifacts before they are packaged and deployed?

choices.text: In a generated .aws-sam/build directory
In a .git/objects folder
Directly overwriting the original source files in the project root
In the account's default CloudTrail log bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
sam build writes built artifacts to the .aws-sam/build directory.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Git objects: no.
• Overwrites sources: no.
• CloudTrail bucket: no.

Key takeaway: SAM build output → .aws-sam/build.

stem: A developer needs to store a frequently changing, hierarchically organized set of non-secret configuration values that several Lambda functions read at runtime, and wants to update those values without redeploying any function code. Compared to Lambda environment variables, why might AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store be the better fit?

choices.text: Lambda environment variables cannot be encrypted under any circumstances
Parameter Store values change without redeploying functions and support hierarchies
Parameter Store is the only mechanism that can pass values into a Lambda function
Lambda environment variables can store only numeric values

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parameter Store supports hierarchical paths, and values can change without redeploying functions that read them at runtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Env vars can't be encrypted: they can.
• Only mechanism: env vars also work.
• Env vars numeric only: false.

Key takeaway: shared, changing, hierarchical config → Parameter Store.

stem: When preparing a containerized application for deployment on Amazon ECS, where does a developer specify the amount of CPU and memory the application's containers require?

choices.text: In the ECS task definition
In the Dockerfile's CMD instruction
In the VPC route table
In the Amazon ECR repository policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Container settings such as image, CPU, memory, ports, and environment are defined in the ECS task definition.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dockerfile CMD: startup command only.
• Route table: networking.
• ECR policy: repository access.

Key takeaway: ECS runtime config → task definition.

stem: A team is rolling out a new feature-flag value using AWS AppConfig and wants to minimize the blast radius if the change causes errors, automatically halting the rollout if a specified CloudWatch alarm enters ALARM state. Which AppConfig capability provides this?

choices.text: A deployment strategy (growth, bake time) plus an alarm rollback
A Lambda alias with weighted traffic routing
An API Gateway stage variable
A CodeDeploy AppSpec lifecycle hook

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An AppConfig deployment strategy with growth rate and bake time rolls out gradually, and an alarm monitor rolls back automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda alias weights: code, not config.
• Stage variables: API settings.
• AppSpec hooks: CodeDeploy.

Key takeaway: gradual config rollout → AppConfig strategy + alarms.

stem: A developer wants to debug a Lambda handler locally with breakpoints, using the same runtime environment as Lambda. Which command fits?

choices.text: sam local invoke with debug port options
sam package to S3
sam validate on the template, then console tests
sam deploy --guided

explanation:
Why this is correct:
sam local invoke runs the function in a Docker container that mimics the Lambda runtime and supports attaching a debugger with debug port options.

Why the other options are wrong:
• deploy: sends to AWS.
• package: uploads artifacts.
• validate: checks template syntax only.

Key takeaway: local runtime emulation → sam local invoke.

stem: A frontend team needs to start building against an API before the backend Lambda functions are implemented. Which API Gateway integration type lets them return static, predefined responses for each method without invoking any backend at all?

choices.text: Lambda proxy integration
HTTP integration
Mock integration
AWS service integration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A mock integration returns responses defined in API Gateway, so frontend teams can build against the API before backends exist.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda proxy: needs the function.
• HTTP integration: needs a backend.
• AWS service integration: calls real services.

Key takeaway: API before backend → mock integration.

stem: An API needs dev, test, and prod environments with different backend Lambda aliases and different throttling, from the same API definition. Which API Gateway feature fits?

choices.text: Stages with stage variables and per-stage throttling
Separate APIs copied and edited for each environment
Usage plans alone, without stages
Different HTTP methods per environment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Stages are named deployments of an API with their own URLs, stage variables (for example, pointing to a Lambda alias), and settings such as throttling and logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate APIs: duplication and drift.
• Methods: not environments.
• Usage plans without stages: plans attach to stages.

Key takeaway: environments of one API → stages + stage variables.

stem: A developer modifies an AWS SAM template to add a new DynamoDB table and wants to update the already-deployed CloudFormation stack with this change while first reviewing what will be modified. Which SAM CLI workflow accomplishes this?

choices.text: Delete and recreate the entire stack for every template change
sam build then sam deploy, reviewing the change set
Add the table manually in the console to match the template
Run sam local start-api, which pushes template changes to the stack

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Run sam build then sam deploy, which creates a CloudFormation change set you can review before updating the stack.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete and recreate: disruptive.
• Manual console changes: drift.
• sam local start-api: local only.

Key takeaway: update SAM stacks → build + deploy.

stem: A Lambda function is triggered by new objects uploaded to an S3 bucket. To test the function's logic in a development environment without uploading a real file, what should the developer do?

choices.text: Invoke the function with no input payload at all
Invoke it with a sample S3 event JSON payload
Change the trigger to a CloudWatch Events rule instead
Delete the S3 event notification configuration before testing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Invoking the function with a sample S3 event JSON (for example, from sam local generate-event) tests its logic realistically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No payload: logic can't run.
• Change trigger: tests something else.
• Delete notifications: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: test with realistic event payloads.

stem: After deploying a new version of a Lambda function to a development stage, a developer notices intermittent errors, but the API Gateway response only shows a generic 500 error. Which combination of tools would most directly help pinpoint where in the request the failure occurs?

choices.text: Amazon Route 53 health checks on the API endpoint
CloudWatch Logs plus X-Ray tracing
Amazon S3 server access logs only
AWS Config rule evaluations for the function

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Logs show errors, and X-Ray tracing shows where failures and latency occur across calls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 checks: availability only.
• S3 access logs: unrelated.
• Config: configuration.

Key takeaway: debug Lambda → logs + traces.

stem: During active development, a developer wants to quickly push iterative code changes to a Lambda function in a dev AWS account for fast feedback, without waiting for a full CloudFormation stack update each time. Which SAM CLI capability is designed for this, and how does it differ from sam deploy?

choices.text: No difference; both commands always perform a full stack update
sam sync, which pushes code directly and deploys fully only for infra changes
sam package, used as a direct substitute for sam sync
sam deploy --fast, which skips all validation checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
sam sync pushes code changes directly to the cloud and does full deployments only when infrastructure changes, speeding iteration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No difference: sync is faster.
• sam package: packaging only.
• --fast flag: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: fast dev iteration → sam sync.

stem: A team wants each API Gateway stage (dev, test, prod) to invoke a different Lambda alias of the same function without maintaining separate API definitions per stage. What is the standard way to achieve this?

choices.text: Use resource policies on the function to redirect requests between aliases
Hardcode the target alias ARN in the function's own code
A stage variable in the integration ARN set per stage
Create a completely separate REST API for each stage

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A stage variable in the integration's function ARN (for example, alias ${stageVariables.alias}) lets each stage call a different alias.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Resource policies redirect: no.
• Hardcode in code: no.
• Separate APIs: duplication.

Key takeaway: per-stage backends → stage variables.

stem: A developer wants to verify that a Lambda function correctly processes custom events published to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, before any real upstream service starts sending such events. What is a straightforward way to test this in development?

choices.text: Publish a sample event with the expected detail-type to the bus
Modify the function's IAM role trust policy to allow EventBridge
Delete the rule and invoke the function with no event at all
Wait for production traffic to trigger the rule naturally

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Publishing a sample event with the expected source and detail-type to the bus triggers the rule and tests the function end to end.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trust policy change: not testing.
• No event: doesn't test the rule.
• Wait for production: not testing.

Key takeaway: test rules with sample events.

stem: A developer wants to test an API locally: send HTTP requests to routes defined in the SAM template and have them hit local function code with hot reloading. Which command fits?

choices.text: sam logs --tail
sam sync against production
sam local start-api
sam local invoke for each route

explanation:
Why this is correct:
sam local start-api runs a local HTTP server emulating API Gateway routes from the template and invokes local function code for each request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• local invoke: runs one function once with an event.
• logs: fetches deployed logs.
• sync to production: not local.

Key takeaway: local API emulation → start-api.

stem: An application's Lambda function calls a third-party payment API during checkout. In the integration test environment, the team replaces calls to the real payment API with a local mock that returns canned responses. What is the main tradeoff of this approach?

choices.text: It removes the need for integration testing before a production release
It eliminates the need to test the application's error-handling paths
Faster, stable tests, but real-API integration issues go uncaught
It guarantees the application behaves identically in production

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mocking the third-party API makes tests fast and stable, but real-API integration issues can go undetected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Removes integration testing: no.
• No error-handling tests: still needed.
• Guarantees production behavior: no.

Key takeaway: mocks trade realism for speed.

stem: A developer runs sam deploy against a dev environment stack that had previously been modified manually in the console (for example, someone changed a Lambda environment variable directly). The deployment now fails with a stack update conflict. What is the most likely underlying cause?

choices.text: The SAM CLI does not support updating existing stacks
Drift: resources no longer match CloudFormation's recorded state
The associated API Gateway stage was deleted by another deployment
The Lambda function has exceeded its reserved concurrency limit

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Manual changes cause drift, so resources no longer match CloudFormation's recorded state and updates can fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SAM can't update stacks: it can.
• Deleted stage: different scenario.
• Reserved concurrency: unrelated.

Key takeaway: manual changes → drift → failed deploys.

stem: A CloudFormation template for an API needs to deploy to dev, test, and prod environments with different values for things like the DynamoDB table name and Lambda memory size, while reusing the same template across all three. What is a standard way to achieve this?

choices.text: Store the values as tags on the stack's S3 template bucket
Parameters or mappings with per-environment values
Hardcode dev values and edit them manually before each production deploy
Maintain three separate, hand-edited copies of the entire template

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parameters or mappings supply per-environment values from one template.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tags on template bucket: no.
• Manual edits: error-prone.
• Three copies: drift.

Key takeaway: one template, many environments → parameters/mappings.

stem: A developer wants to send only 10% of live traffic to a new version of a Lambda function while the remaining 90% continues to go to the current stable version, to validate the new version's behavior with real traffic before fully promoting it. What Lambda feature enables this?

choices.text: A second, separately named function invoked at random by client code
A weighted alias across two versions
An API Gateway usage plan with a throttling limit
A Lambda layer version constraint on the function

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A weighted alias splits traffic between two versions (for example, 90/10).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Random second function: unmanaged.
• Usage plan: throttling.
• Layer constraint: dependencies.

Key takeaway: traffic splitting in Lambda → weighted aliases.

stem: A team deploys a Lambda function packaged as a container image and wants each deployment to be uniquely and traceably identified in Amazon ECR, while allowing easy rollback to any previous deployment. What practice best supports this?

choices.text: Always deploy using only the latest tag
Immutable, uniquely tagged images (e.g., commit SHA)
Store the image contents in a Lambda environment variable
Disable ECR image scanning to speed up deployments

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable, uniquely tagged images (for example, by commit SHA) make each deployment traceable and reproducible.

Why the other options are wrong:
• latest tag: changes underneath.
• Image in env variable: nonsense.
• Disable scanning: unrelated.

Key takeaway: traceable images → unique immutable tags.

stem: A team connects its repo to Amplify Hosting. It wants every feature branch deployed to its own URL, previews for pull requests, and password protection for non-production branches. Which setup fits?

choices.text: One Amplify app that deploys only the main branch
Branch auto-detection, PR previews, access control
A manual zip upload to Amplify for each branch
S3 static hosting with a CloudFront distribution per branch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amplify Hosting can automatically connect branches (by pattern), deploy each to its own URL, create previews for pull requests, and restrict access to branches with passwords.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual zip: no CI/CD.
• Main only: misses the branch requirement.
• S3 per branch: rebuilds what Amplify offers.

Key takeaway: branch-based frontend hosting → Amplify.

stem: Before applying an update to a production CloudFormation stack, a developer wants to preview exactly which resources will be modified, replaced, or deleted. Which CloudFormation feature should they use?

choices.text: A stack policy
A change set
A drift detection report
A nested stack

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A change set previews exactly which resources will be added, modified, or replaced before executing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stack policy: protects resources.
• Drift report: compares current state.
• Nested stack: structure.

Key takeaway: preview updates → change sets.

stem: How does AWS SAM relate to AWS CloudFormation when defining and deploying serverless application infrastructure as code?

choices.text: SAM can deploy only container workloads and cannot define Lambda functions
CloudFormation cannot deploy Lambda functions; only AWS SAM can
SAM replaces CloudFormation entirely and does not use it underneath
SAM shorthand is transformed into CloudFormation resources

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAM is a CloudFormation transform: its shorthand expands into standard CloudFormation resources at deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Containers only: no.
• CloudFormation can't deploy Lambda: it can.
• Replaces CloudFormation: uses it.

Key takeaway: SAM = CloudFormation extension.

stem: A team tests API changes in the test stage of an API Gateway REST API and, once validated, wants to promote that exact same tested configuration to the prod stage without redefining the API's methods and integrations from scratch. What should they do?

choices.text: Create a deployment and associate it with the prod stage
Delete the test stage before a prod stage can be created
Recreate every resource and method in a new API for production
Change the API's protocol from REST to HTTP as part of promotion

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Create a deployment of the tested API configuration and associate it with the prod stage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete test stage: unnecessary.
• Recreate API: unnecessary.
• Change protocol: unrelated.

Key takeaway: promote via deployments to stages.

stem: A developer wants unit tests generated for an existing Lambda handler, including edge cases, directly in the IDE, then reviewed before commit. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Use CloudFormation to generate test stubs
Run CodeGuru Profiler to create test files from runtime profiles
Enable X-Ray, which produces tests from traces
Ask Amazon Q Developer to generate tests, then review them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Q Developer can generate unit tests from code in the IDE. The developer should still review and adjust them, especially assertions and edge cases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: traces, not tests.
• Profiler: performance profiling.
• CloudFormation: infrastructure.

Key takeaway: AI-generated tests speed up work, but review them before trusting them.

stem: A CI/CD pipeline needs to automatically run a project's unit and integration test suite on every commit-triggered build, failing the pipeline if any test fails. Where should the test commands be defined for an AWS CodeBuild project?

choices.text: In buildspec.yml (pre_build or build phase)
In the Lambda function's environment variables
In the artifact store bucket's resource policy
In the API Gateway stage's description field

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Test commands go in buildspec.yml phases (pre_build or build), so CodeBuild runs them on every commit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda env vars: no.
• Bucket policy: no.
• Stage description: no.

Key takeaway: CI tests → buildspec phases.

stem: A team is deciding whether to run pre-production tests against a Lambda function's $LATEST unqualified version or against a published version referenced by an alias. What is a key tradeoff of testing directly against $LATEST?

choices.text: An alias can never be pointed at $LATEST
$LATEST cannot be invoked under any circumstances
$LATEST can change anytime, so results aren't reproducible
Published versions cannot be invoked for testing; only $LATEST can

explanation:
Why this is correct:
$LATEST can change at any time, so test results aren't reproducible. Test a published version (via an alias).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Alias can't point to $LATEST: it can.
• $LATEST can't be invoked: it can.
• Versions can't be invoked: they can.

Key takeaway: test immutable versions.

stem: An automated test suite for an API Gateway deployment fails only in the test environment, and investigation shows the test scripts reference a Lambda function ARN copied directly from the dev environment's console rather than derived from the target environment's own stack. What is the best fix to prevent this class of failure going forward?

choices.text: Read resource IDs from the stack outputs per environment
Disable the test environment's API Gateway stage
Merge the dev and test environments into one AWS account
Grant the test suite full administrator IAM permissions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tests failing in one environment because of hardcoded IDs should read resource IDs from each environment's stack outputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable stage: avoids the problem.
• Merge environments: loses isolation.
• Admin permissions: unrelated.

Key takeaway: environment-specific values → stack outputs.

stem: A Lambda function's dependencies reach 1.2 GB unzipped and exceed the zip limit. Cold starts must remain reasonable. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Increase ephemeral storage to hold the dependencies
Download dependencies from S3 on every invocation
Package it as a container image in ECR
Split the dependencies into five layers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Container images up to 10 GB are supported, and Lambda caches image layers, so larger dependencies are workable. Layers count toward the 250 MB unzipped limit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Five layers: still within the same 250 MB total limit.
• Download per invocation: slow and costly.
• Ephemeral storage: runtime space, not package size.

Key takeaway: large dependencies → container image.

stem: A company wants their API Gateway API to be reachable at api.example.com instead of the default execute-api URL, using their own TLS certificate. Which combination of AWS features accomplishes this?

choices.text: Enable AWS WAF on the API
A custom domain with an ACM certificate and a Route 53 alias
Rename the API Gateway stage itself to api.example.com
Use an S3 bucket policy to rewrite the API's hostname

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom domain name in API Gateway with an ACM certificate, plus a Route 53 alias record, serves the API at api.example.com.

Why the other options are wrong:
• WAF: security.
• Rename the stage: not a domain.
• S3 policy: unrelated.

Key takeaway: friendly API URL → custom domain.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a blue/green deployment strategy from a canary deployment strategy?

choices.text: Blue/green switches to a separate environment; canary shifts a small share first
Canary always replaces the underlying infrastructure, while blue/green never does
Blue/green and canary are two names for the exact same technique
Blue/green works only with Lambda, and canary only with EC2

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Blue/green switches traffic to a separate new environment. Canary shifts a small portion of traffic to the new version first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Canary replaces infrastructure: no.
• Same technique: no.
• Service-specific: both apply broadly.

Key takeaway: blue/green = switch; canary = gradual sample.

stem: A pipeline currently polls CodeCommit for changes and sometimes starts 10 minutes late. The team wants near-immediate starts. Which change fits?

choices.text: Shorten the polling interval to 1 second
Schedule StartPipelineExecution every 5 minutes
Add a manual approval at the start of the pipeline
Use an EventBridge-based change detection trigger

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Event-based change detection starts the pipeline as soon as the push event arrives, instead of waiting for the next poll.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 1-second polling: not configurable, and wasteful.
• Manual approval: adds delay.
• 5-minute schedule: still delayed and wasteful.

Key takeaway: prefer event-driven triggers over polling.

stem: A company wants their deployment pipeline to automatically build and deploy to a test environment, but require a human to manually approve before that same build proceeds to deploy into production. Which AWS CodePipeline feature supports this?

choices.text: A Lambda function with no attached IAM permissions
A manual approval stage before production
An API Gateway resource policy
A CodeBuild buildspec artifacts section

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A manual approval stage before production pauses the pipeline until someone approves.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda without permissions: no.
• API resource policy: no.
• Artifacts section: packaging.

Key takeaway: human gate → manual approval action.

stem: During a Lambda deployment managed by AWS CodeDeploy, an associated CloudWatch alarm monitoring function error rate enters ALARM state partway through the traffic shift. What does CodeDeploy do if automatic rollback is enabled for that alarm?

choices.text: CodeDeploy ignores the alarm and continues shifting traffic to completion
CodeDeploy pauses indefinitely until the stack is deleted manually
CodeDeploy immediately deletes the Lambda function entirely
It stops and rolls traffic back to the prior version

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When an associated alarm fires, CodeDeploy stops the deployment and rolls traffic back to the previous version (if configured).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ignores alarm: no.
• Pauses indefinitely: no.
• Deletes the function: no.

Key takeaway: alarms trigger automatic rollback.

stem: A team needs instant rollback for a Lambda function and wants callers never to change the ARN they call. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Publish versions; callers use an alias you repoint
Deploy code to $LATEST and redeploy the old zip on failure
Create a new function name per release
Use layers to hold each release's code

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Published versions are immutable snapshots of code and configuration. Callers invoke an alias ARN, and repointing the alias to the previous version gives instant rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• $LATEST redeploy: slow, and the old state may not be reproducible.
• New function names: callers must change ARNs.
• Layers: share code; they don't version releases.

Key takeaway: immutable versions + movable alias.

stem: A CloudFormation stack update fails partway through because a new resource property is invalid. What does CloudFormation do by default in this situation?

choices.text: It leaves the stack half-updated indefinitely with no further action
It rolls back to the previous working state
It ignores the failure and marks the update as successful
It deletes the entire stack and all of its resources

explanation:
Why this is correct:
By default, a failed stack update rolls back to the previous working state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Half-updated forever: no.
• Marks success: no.
• Deletes stack: no.

Key takeaway: CloudFormation updates are transactional.

stem: A team runs a containerized application on Amazon ECS and wants to perform a blue/green deployment where a new task set is deployed alongside the old one, traffic is shifted via a load balancer, and the old task set is only terminated after validation succeeds. Which AWS service is designed to orchestrate this ECS blue/green deployment pattern?

choices.text: AWS Config
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Inspector
AWS CodeDeploy (ECS platform)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy's ECS compute platform performs blue/green deployments with traffic shifting between task sets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config, Trusted Advisor, Inspector: not deployment tools.

Key takeaway: ECS blue/green → CodeDeploy.

stem: A team is choosing between a canary deployment configuration, where a small initial percentage of traffic is held for a wait period and then the rest shifts all at once, and a linear deployment configuration, where traffic increases in small, equal increments over multiple steps, for a Lambda function update. What is the key tradeoff between the two?

choices.text: Linear can't use automatic rollback, but canary always can
Canary: one small step then all; linear: gradual steps, slower but safer
Canary deployments are available only for EC2, not for Lambda
Canary and linear always take the same total time to complete

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Canary shifts a small portion once, then the rest. Linear shifts in equal steps over time, which is slower but more gradual.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Linear can't roll back: it can.
• Canary EC2-only: available for Lambda and ECS.
• Same total time: differs.

Key takeaway: canary = two steps; linear = many steps.

stem: A pipeline uploads a new Lambda zip to S3 with the same key each time, and the CloudFormation update shows no changes. Why, and what fixes it?

choices.text: Unchanged key means no diff; use a new key or object version
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration so CloudFormation detects the upload
Delete and recreate the stack every release
CloudFormation never updates Lambda code

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation updates function code only when the Code properties (S3Key or S3ObjectVersion) change. Using a unique key (for example, a commit hash) or the object version triggers the update.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never updates: it does when properties change.
• Transfer Acceleration: unrelated.
• Recreate the stack: causes downtime and is unnecessary.

Key takeaway: change the artifact reference to trigger deployment.

stem: During an incident, a developer needs the 20 most recent log events containing ERROR, newest first. Which Logs Insights query is correct?

choices.text: fields @timestamp, @message | sort @timestamp asc | filter @message like /ERROR/ | limit 20
stats count(*) by bin(5m) | filter @message like /ERROR/
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message = "ERROR" | limit 20

explanation:
Why this is correct:
filter with like /ERROR/ matches substrings, sort @timestamp desc puts the newest first, and limit 20 returns 20 events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ascending sort: returns the oldest first.
• = "ERROR": matches only messages that are exactly 'ERROR'.
• stats: aggregates counts; it doesn't return events.

Key takeaway: filter → sort → limit.

stem: A CodeDeploy deployment to an EC2/On-Premises deployment group fails during the AllowTraffic lifecycle event and is automatically rolled back. Where should a developer look first to determine why instances failed to start receiving traffic?

choices.text: The VPC Flow Logs for the subnet hosting the instances
The CloudTrail event history for the pipeline's IAM role
CodeDeploy events and target group health status
The S3 access logs for the application revision bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AllowTraffic failures usually mean instances fail load balancer health checks. Check CodeDeploy events and target group health status.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: rarely first.
• CloudTrail for pipeline role: unrelated.
• Bucket access logs: unrelated.

Key takeaway: AllowTraffic failures → target health.

stem: Messages processed by a Lambda function triggered from an SQS queue are increasingly landing in the configured dead-letter queue. CloudWatch Logs show no application errors, but invocation duration is consistently close to the function's timeout. Which tool would best confirm whether a downstream HTTP call inside the function is causing the delay?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor, by reviewing its performance checks
AWS X-Ray active tracing and subsegment timings
Contributor Insights, identifying top contributors to queue depth
Logs Insights, running stats count() grouped by log stream

explanation:
Why this is correct:
X-Ray tracing with subsegment timings shows which downstream call makes processing exceed limits, causing DLQ arrivals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: no.
• Contributor Insights: top contributors, not timing.
• Logs Insights counts: no timing breakdown.

Key takeaway: find slow steps → X-Ray subsegments.

stem: During an incident, on-call engineers must see error rate, latency, recent deploy markers, and related log queries together, across 3 Regions. Which setup fits?

choices.text: An S3 export of logs reviewed after the incident
A cross-Region CloudWatch dashboard
A separate dashboard per Region opened side by side
CloudTrail event history filtered by service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch dashboards can show widgets from multiple Regions, including metrics, alarm status, and Logs Insights results, giving one correlated view.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate per Region: slows correlation.
• CloudTrail: API activity only.
• After-the-fact export: not usable during response.

Key takeaway: one correlated view for incident response.

stem: In the X-Ray service map for a microservices application, one downstream service node is shown in red with a much higher average response time than its neighbors, while the client-facing service shows normal error rates but elevated latency. What does this most likely indicate?

choices.text: Red means the downstream service is throttling API Gateway requests
The downstream service is the bottleneck
X-Ray sampling is misconfigured and producing inaccurate map data
The client-facing service has a memory leak unrelated to dependencies

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A red node in the service map shows the downstream service returning errors or faults, indicating it's the bottleneck.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Throttling API Gateway: not implied.
• Sampling misconfigured: no.
• Client memory leak: unrelated.

Key takeaway: service map colors show where errors originate.

stem: A Lambda function fronted by API Gateway intermittently returns HTTP 502 errors. CloudWatch Logs for the function occasionally show an unhandled exception with a stack trace, but only for a fraction of the failing requests. What is the most effective way to correlate a specific client-reported failure with its exact Lambda log entry?

choices.text: Ask the client to keep retrying until the request eventually succeeds
Increase the function's memory
Enable execution logging and correlate by request ID
Delete older log streams so only the most recent errors remain

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enabling API Gateway execution logging and correlating by request ID reveals malformed Lambda responses that cause 502s.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Retry: hides the bug.
• More memory: unlikely cause.
• Delete logs: loses evidence.

Key takeaway: 502 from Lambda proxy → inspect execution logs.

stem: A developer wants to find which API endpoint generated the most 5xx errors over the past 24 hours using CloudWatch Logs Insights on a log group where every request logs an endpoint field and a statusCode field. Which query fragment achieves this?

choices.text: fields endpoint, statusCode | sort statusCode desc | limit 1
stats avg(statusCode) by endpoint
fields endpoint, statusCode | filter statusCode >= 500 | stats count(*) as errorCount by endpoint | sort errorCount desc
filter endpoint like /5/ | stats count(*) by statusCode

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Filter statusCode >= 500, count by endpoint, sort descending, and limit to find the endpoint with the most 5xx errors.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sort by status: not counts.
• Average status: meaningless.
• Regex on endpoint: wrong field.

Key takeaway: top errors → filter + stats count + sort.

stem: A stack is stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED because a resource was deleted manually. The team needs the stack usable again without deleting it. Which action fits?

choices.text: Edit the stack state in the console's resource list
ContinueUpdateRollback, skipping the resource
Delete and recreate every resource from scratch
Wait for CloudFormation to retry automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ContinueUpdateRollback resumes the rollback, and ResourcesToSkip lets it skip resources that can't roll back (such as manually deleted ones), returning the stack to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Editing state: not possible.
• Recreating: destructive and unnecessary.
• Waiting: it doesn't retry by itself.

Key takeaway: stuck rollback → continue-update-rollback (skip if needed).

stem: Compared to instrumenting a Lambda function with direct calls to the CloudWatch PutMetricData API, what is a key operational advantage of using the CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF)?

choices.text: EMF metrics support more dimensions per metric than PutMetricData
EMF comes from logs asynchronously, avoiding API calls and latency
EMF creates a CloudWatch alarm for every metric it emits
EMF is the only method that supports one-second custom metrics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMF metrics are extracted from logs asynchronously, avoiding PutMetricData calls and their latency and throttling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More dimensions: not the main benefit.
• Creates alarms: no.
• Only 1-second method: no.

Key takeaway: Lambda metrics → EMF.

stem: Clients calling an API Gateway REST API protected by a Lambda authorizer begin receiving HTTP 403 Forbidden responses after a recent deployment, and the backend Lambda function's own logs show no invocations at all. Where should the developer look to determine why requests are being rejected before reaching the backend?

choices.text: The AWS Config configuration history for the API resource
The backend Lambda function's logs
API Gateway execution logs (authorizer results)
The S3 server access logs for the API Gateway stage

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway execution logs show the authorizer's result and policy, explaining 403 responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config history: no.
• Backend logs: requests never reached it.
• S3 access logs: unrelated.

Key takeaway: authorizer denials → execution logs.

stem: A request intermittently takes 8 seconds. Metrics show the latency spike, logs show a timeout message, but the team can't tell which of 6 services caused it. Which signal should they use next?

choices.text: CloudTrail data events enabled for each service in the request path
More CloudWatch metrics at 1-second resolution
X-Ray traces showing time spent per service segment
Longer log retention on all log groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Metrics show that something is wrong and logs show events, but traces show where time went across services for a single request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More metrics: still aggregates, not per request.
• Longer retention: doesn't locate the slow hop.
• CloudTrail: AWS API calls, not the request path.

Key takeaway: metrics = what, logs = detail, traces = where.

stem: A team has dashboards for known failure modes but spent hours diagnosing a new, unexpected issue. Which improvement reflects observability rather than monitoring?

choices.text: A bigger dashboard with every existing metric
Shorter alarm evaluation periods
More static threshold alarms for known errors
Rich, correlated telemetry for new questions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Monitoring watches predefined signals. Observability means emitting enough high-cardinality, correlated data to ask new questions about unknown failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More thresholds, bigger dashboards, shorter periods: all improve monitoring of known issues only.

Key takeaway: observability = explore the unknown; monitoring = watch the known.

stem: An app must publish CheckoutLatency with dimension Environment=Production at 1-second resolution. Metric calls must not slow down requests. Which approach fits?

choices.text: X-Ray annotations as metrics
Synchronous PutMetricData on every request
EMF logs with StorageResolution 1
A metric filter counting log lines

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The embedded metric format writes metrics in structured logs, which CloudWatch extracts asynchronously, including dimensions and high-resolution storage, so requests don't wait on API calls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Synchronous PutMetricData: adds latency and can throttle.
• Metric filters: produce standard-resolution counts.
• X-Ray annotations: for filtering traces, not metrics.

Key takeaway: custom metrics without request latency → EMF.

stem: When instrumenting code with AWS X-Ray, a developer needs to attach data to a trace that will be indexed so it can be used to filter traces in the X-Ray console, for example filtering all traces for a specific customerId. Which feature should be used, and how does it differ from the alternative?

choices.text: Both are indexed identically
Annotations, which are indexed and filterable
Metadata, which is indexed, while annotations are display-only
Subsegments, the only element that supports key-value filtering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Annotations are indexed key-value pairs you can filter traces by. Metadata isn't indexed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Indexed identically: no.
• Metadata indexed: reversed.
• Subsegments only: no.

Key takeaway: searchable trace data → annotations.

stem: A team switches their application's log output from unstructured plain-text lines to structured JSON log entries. What is the primary observability benefit of this change?

choices.text: Fields can be reliably filtered and aggregated in Logs Insights
JSON logs compress automatically, reducing storage costs to zero
Structured logs are encrypted automatically with a customer managed KMS key
Structured logging removes the need for a log retention policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Structured JSON logs let Logs Insights discover fields automatically, so you can filter and aggregate reliably.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic compression: no.
• Automatic CMK encryption: no.
• No retention policy: still needed.

Key takeaway: structured logs → queryable fields.

stem: A containerized application on Amazon ECS defines a container-level health check in its task definition and a separate readiness endpoint checked by an Application Load Balancer target group before routing traffic. What is the key difference in purpose between these two checks?

choices.text: They serve the same purpose, so one of them should always be removed
The target group check restarts containers; the container check routes traffic
The container check drives scale-in; the target group check controls IAM
Container check: liveness/restart; target group check: readiness for traffic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The container health check determines liveness and triggers restarts. The target group health check determines readiness to receive traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same purpose: different.
• Swapped roles: incorrect.
• Scale-in driver: no.

Key takeaway: liveness vs. readiness.

stem: On-call engineers for a multi-service application are being repeatedly paged for cascading failures that stem from one root cause, creating alert fatigue from dozens of individual CloudWatch Alarms. Select TWO CloudWatch capabilities that directly help reduce this kind of alert noise.

choices.text: Shorten every alarm's evaluation period to the minimum
Publish a separate SNS notification for every metric datapoint
Composite alarms combining existing alarms
Anomaly detection instead of fixed thresholds
Disable all alarms outside business hours

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Composite alarms page on combined root symptoms, and anomaly detection avoids static thresholds that fire during normal variation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shorter periods: more noise.
• SNS per datapoint: more noise.
• Disable after hours: dangerous.

Key takeaway: reduce paging noise → composite + anomaly detection.

stem: A team runs a .NET app on EC2 with SQL Server and wants automatic detection of common problems, with correlated metrics and logs grouped into problem views, with minimal setup. Which service fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Application Insights
AWS Config conformance packs
Amazon Inspector application assessments
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Application Insights sets up monitoring for supported application stacks (such as .NET and SQL Server), detects anomalies, and groups correlated metrics and logs into problems.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration compliance.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.

Key takeaway: app-aware automatic problem detection → Application Insights.

stem: A trading application needs a custom CloudWatch metric to be usable for alarming within seconds of being published, instead of the default one-minute granularity. What must the developer do when publishing this metric?

choices.text: Nothing extra; all custom metrics are available at 1-second granularity
Use Logs Insights, the only way to get sub-minute granularity
Publish with StorageResolution = 1
Enable X-Ray active tracing on the metric's data source

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Publishing with StorageResolution = 1 creates a high-resolution metric usable for alarms with 10-second periods.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All metrics 1-second: default is 60.
• Logs Insights only: no.
• X-Ray: unrelated.

Key takeaway: seconds-level alarms → high-resolution metrics.

stem: An ECS service behind an Application Load Balancer passes its health check endpoint, which simply returns HTTP 200 immediately after each task starts, but requests routed to newly started tasks fail for several seconds because the task has not yet finished loading a local cache. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Remove the health check so traffic is never blocked
Lower the task's CPU allocation so the cache loads faster
Increase the ALB idle timeout setting
Make the health check confirm startup dependencies are ready

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The health check should confirm startup dependencies (such as the cache) are ready before the task receives traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove health check: unsafe.
• Lower CPU: slower.
• Idle timeout: unrelated.

Key takeaway: health checks should reflect readiness.

stem: A payment function must never be starved by other functions and must avoid cold starts during business hours. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: More memory, which reserves capacity
Provisioned concurrency only, which also caps others
Reserved plus scheduled provisioned concurrency
Reserved concurrency only, which also pre-warms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reserved concurrency guarantees (and caps) a function's share of account concurrency. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized; Application Auto Scaling can schedule it for business hours.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reserved only: doesn't pre-warm.
• Provisioned only: doesn't reserve account concurrency against other functions.
• Memory: affects CPU, not concurrency.

Key takeaway: reserved = guarantee and cap; provisioned = warm.

stem: A Lambda function that processes orders begins returning ThrottlingException errors during a traffic spike, even though the account-level concurrent execution limit has not been reached. The function's Throttles metric in CloudWatch is increasing. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Reserved concurrency is set below current demand
The function's memory allocation is set too high
The function uses an unsupported runtime version
The execution role is missing a required permission

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reserved concurrency set below demand causes throttling during spikes. Raise it or remove the cap.

Why the other options are wrong:
• High memory: doesn't cause throttling.
• Unsupported runtime: different error.
• Missing permission: AccessDenied, not throttling.

Key takeaway: throttling → concurrency limits.

stem: A developer wants to determine the memory configuration that minimizes cost while keeping execution duration acceptable for a compute-intensive Lambda function, automatically testing many memory settings rather than manually. Which approach best fits this need?

choices.text: Enable provisioned concurrency
Set memory to the maximum, since more memory always minimizes cost
Lambda Power Tuning to compare cost and duration
Use Trusted Advisor, which identifies the optimal Lambda memory setting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Lambda Power Tuning runs the function at several memory sizes and compares cost and duration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned concurrency: cold starts.
• Max memory always cheapest: not always.
• Trusted Advisor: not this.

Key takeaway: optimize memory → Power Tuning.

stem: A team wants to automatically stream every log event containing the word FATAL from a CloudWatch Logs group to a Lambda function in near real time for automated incident creation, without processing every other log line. Which feature should they configure?

choices.text: A saved Logs Insights query scheduled to run every minute
An S3 event notification on the log group's export bucket
A subscription filter on FATAL to the Lambda function
An X-Ray sampling rule that samples only FATAL-tagged traces

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A subscription filter matching FATAL streams those events to the Lambda function in near real time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled queries: delayed.
• S3 export notifications: delayed.
• X-Ray sampling: traces.

Key takeaway: stream matching logs → subscription filters.

stem: An API behind CloudFront returns different content by Accept-Language. Users see the wrong language. Which fix fits?

choices.text: Add Accept-Language to the cache key via the cache policy
Set Cache-Control: no-store on all responses
Disable compression on the distribution
Rely on ETag headers to separate the language variants in cache

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches one object per cache key. Including Accept-Language in the cache policy creates separate cached variants per language (normalizing values helps hit ratio).

Why the other options are wrong:
• no-store: disables caching entirely.
• Compression: unrelated.
• ETag: validates freshness, not variants.

Key takeaway: responses vary by a header → put that header in the cache key.

stem: An RDS-backed application has slow response times only during peak hours. A developer enables Amazon RDS Performance Insights and sees that a small number of SQL queries account for the vast majority of database load during those periods. What should the developer do next to pinpoint the performance bottleneck?

choices.text: Examine top SQL waits in Performance Insights and optimize or index
Disable Performance Insights, since it reports only symptoms, not causes
Delete slow query log entries so a lower baseline load is calculated
Increase the instance size immediately

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Performance Insights shows top SQL and wait events during peaks. Optimize those queries or indexes first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable it: loses insight.
• Delete slow logs: hides problems.
• Bigger instance first: may not fix bad queries.

Key takeaway: diagnose before scaling.

stem: A team is comparing API Gateway's built-in response caching with using Amazon CloudFront in front of their API to reduce backend load. Which statement accurately describes a difference between the two?

choices.text: API Gateway caches at global edges, while CloudFront is limited to one Region
API Gateway caches per stage near the API; CloudFront caches at edges
CloudFront caches only static S3 content and can't front API Gateway
They are functionally identical, with no difference in scope

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway caches per stage in the API's Region. CloudFront caches at edge locations near users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reversed: incorrect.
• CloudFront can't front APIs: it can.
• Identical: different scope.

Key takeaway: Regional cache vs. edge cache.

stem: A subscription filter uses the pattern ?ERROR ?WARN on a log group streaming to Kinesis. What reaches Kinesis?

choices.text: Events containing both ERROR and WARN
All events, with ERROR/WARN duplicated
Only events containing ERROR or WARN
Events without ERROR or WARN are deleted from the group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
In filter patterns, ? means OR, so events matching either term are delivered. Other events stay in the log group but aren't forwarded.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All events: filters limit what's sent.
• Both terms: that would require an AND pattern.
• Deletion: filters never delete events.

Key takeaway: ? = OR in filter patterns.

stem: A Java service's CPU is high in production, and the team wants to find which methods consume the most CPU and latency continuously, with low overhead. Which tool fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Container Insights
AWS X-Ray service map
Amazon Inspector
Amazon CodeGuru Profiler

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeGuru Profiler samples running applications with low overhead and shows the methods using the most CPU and latency (flame graphs), with recommendations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: request flow between services, not method-level CPU.
• Container Insights: resource metrics.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: method-level hotspots → CodeGuru Profiler.

stem: A Lambda function consumes an SQS standard queue and charges customer cards. Occasionally the same message is delivered twice, causing double charges. What is the MOST robust fix?

choices.text: Make the handler idempotent with a conditional write on a payment key.
Switch the function's runtime to one with faster startup.
Set the Lambda batch size to 1 so each message is handled alone.
Increase the queue's message retention period.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SQS standard is at-least-once, so the same message can arrive twice. An idempotent handler (for example, a conditional write on a payment ID) prevents double charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Faster runtime: doesn't prevent duplicates.
• Batch size 1: duplicates still possible.
• Retention period: unrelated.

Key takeaway: at-least-once delivery → idempotency.

stem: Two users can edit the same DynamoDB item at the same time, and one user's changes sometimes silently overwrite the other's. The team wants to reject stale updates without locking. What should the developer implement?

choices.text: Optimistic locking with a version attribute and a condition.
Use BatchWriteItem for all updates to the item.
Use strongly consistent reads before every update.
Enable DynamoDB Streams to detect overwrites afterward.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Optimistic locking with a version attribute and a condition expression rejects writes based on stale data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BatchWriteItem: no conditions.
• Strong reads: don't prevent concurrent writes.
• Streams: detect after the fact.

Key takeaway: lost updates → optimistic locking.

stem: A table's partition key is orderId. The application now needs to query orders by customerId sorted by orderDate. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: A local secondary index can be added to the existing table at any time with customerId as its partition key.
Global secondary indexes always share the base table's partition key.
A Scan with a FilterExpression on customerId is as efficient as a Query on an index.
A global secondary index with customerId as partition key and orderDate as sort key supports the query.
Queries on a global secondary index support only eventually consistent reads.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A GSI with customerId as partition key (and a sort attribute) enables the new query, and GSI queries are eventually consistent.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Add LSI later: only at creation.
• GSI shares partition key: no.
• Scan as efficient: no.

Key takeaway: new access pattern → GSI.

stem: A Lambda function processes SQS messages in batches of 10. When one message fails, the entire batch is retried, and successfully processed messages are reprocessed. How can the developer avoid this?

choices.text: Switch the event source to a FIFO queue.
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures and return failed IDs.
Delete all messages manually at the start of the handler.
Increase the visibility timeout to 12 hours.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ReportBatchItemFailures lets the function return only failed message IDs, so successful messages aren't reprocessed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• FIFO: doesn't solve partial failures.
• Delete all first: loses failed messages.
• 12-hour timeout: delays retries.

Key takeaway: partial batch failures → ReportBatchItemFailures.

stem: An IoT backend must orchestrate a 3-step validation for about 50,000 events per second. Each workflow finishes in under 2 seconds, and at-least-once execution is acceptable. Cost must be minimized. Which workflow type fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Batch jobs.
Step Functions Standard workflows.
Step Functions Express workflows.
An EC2 instance running a custom scheduler.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions Express workflows handle very high event rates for short workflows at low cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Batch: batch jobs.
• Standard workflows: lower throughput and higher cost for this rate.
• Custom scheduler on EC2: operations burden.

Key takeaway: high-volume short workflows → Express.

stem: A single-page app authenticates users with an Amazon Cognito user pool. The developer wants an API Gateway HTTP API to reject requests without a valid user pool token, with no custom code. What should be configured?

choices.text: A JWT authorizer using the user pool as issuer.
A Lambda authorizer that decodes and verifies the JWT manually.
An API key required on every route of the API.
IAM authorization with SigV4 signing in the browser.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An HTTP API JWT authorizer with the Cognito user pool as issuer validates tokens without custom code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom Lambda authorizer: unnecessary code.
• API keys: not user authentication.
• SigV4 in browser: requires AWS credentials.

Key takeaway: Cognito JWTs → JWT authorizer.

stem: An application must encrypt 5 MB files client-side using a KMS key. The developer calls the KMS Encrypt API and receives an error. What is the correct approach?

choices.text: Request a KMS quota increase for the Encrypt payload size.
Use an asymmetric KMS key instead of a symmetric one.
Envelope encryption with a GenerateDataKey data key.
Split the file into 4 KB chunks and call Encrypt for each.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KMS Encrypt handles only 4 KB. Envelope encryption generates a data key, encrypts the 5 MB file locally, and stores the encrypted key with it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Quota increase: not possible.
• Asymmetric key: same limits.
• 4 KB chunks: slow and costly.

Key takeaway: large data → envelope encryption.

stem: A high-traffic Lambda function reads a database password from Secrets Manager on every invocation, adding latency and API cost. The password is rotated monthly. What is the recommended improvement?

choices.text: Cache the secret with a TTL (extension or caching client).
Hardcode the password in an environment variable.
Store the password in the deployment package.
Increase the function's memory to speed up the API call.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Caching the secret with a TTL (the Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension or a caching client) cuts API calls and latency while still picking up rotations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcode in env var: loses rotation.
• Package: insecure.
• More memory: doesn't reduce calls.

Key takeaway: frequent secret reads → cache with TTL.

stem: A web application must let authenticated users upload files up to 100 MB directly from the browser to a private S3 bucket, without routing file bytes through the backend and without giving users AWS credentials. What should the developer do?

choices.text: Make the bucket public-write for one hour each day.
Send the file through API Gateway and Lambda to S3.
Embed an IAM user's access key in the JavaScript bundle.
A short-lived presigned URL for a direct upload.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A short-lived presigned URL lets the browser upload directly to S3 without passing large files through API Gateway and Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public write: insecure.
• Through API Gateway: payload limits.
• Embedded key: insecure.

Key takeaway: browser uploads → presigned URLs.

stem: A REST API uses Lambda proxy integration. CORS is enabled in the API Gateway console, and preflight OPTIONS requests succeed, but browser GET requests still fail with a CORS error. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The API stage has not enabled caching.
The Lambda function timeout is too short.
The response lacks Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
The browser requires an API key for the request.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With Lambda proxy integration, the function must return Access-Control-Allow-Origin in its response. Console CORS covers only the preflight.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Caching: unrelated.
• Timeout: different error.
• API key: unrelated to CORS.

Key takeaway: proxy integration → CORS headers from the function.

stem: A developer iterates on a serverless app with Lambda functions and Step Functions. Each full CloudFormation deployment takes several minutes, slowing testing against real cloud resources in a dev account. Which approach speeds up the inner loop the MOST?

choices.text: Increase the Lambda function timeout.
sam sync --watch to the dev stack.
Delete and recreate the stack for every change.
Run sam deploy with --no-execute-changeset.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
sam sync --watch detects changes and pushes code updates quickly, avoiding full CloudFormation deployments for each edit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Timeout: unrelated.
• Recreate stack: slower.
• --no-execute-changeset: doesn't deploy.

Key takeaway: fast iteration → sam sync --watch.

stem: An Elastic Beanstalk environment must stay at full capacity during deployments, and a failed deployment must be rolled back quickly without affecting existing instances. Which deployment policy fits BEST?

choices.text: Immutable.
Rolling with an additional batch.
All at once.
Rolling.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable deployments launch new instances in a temporary group, keep full capacity, and roll back by terminating the new instances if they fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling with batch: rollback is slower.
• All at once: downtime.
• Rolling: reduced capacity.

Key takeaway: full capacity + clean rollback → immutable.

stem: A networking stack creates a VPC, and several application stacks need its subnet IDs. The team wants the application stacks to reference them without hardcoding. Which approach fits, and what is its side effect?

choices.text: Fn::GetAtt across stacks; the network stack can be deleted freely.
Export/ImportValue; exports in use can't change or be deleted.
Parameters with defaults copied from the console, updated automatically.
Mappings in the application stacks, updated when the VPC changes.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exporting subnet IDs from the network stack and importing them with Fn::ImportValue shares values, and exports in use can't be changed or deleted.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GetAtt across stacks: not supported.
• Parameters copied: stale.
• Mappings: static.

Key takeaway: cross-stack sharing → Export/ImportValue.

stem: A Python Lambda function needs machine learning libraries totaling 1.8 GB unzipped. Deployment fails because of package size limits. What should the developer do?

choices.text: Compress the libraries with a higher zip compression level.
Split the libraries across five Lambda layers.
Use a container image (up to 10 GB) in ECR.
Increase the function's ephemeral storage to 10 GB.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Container images support up to 10 GB, enough for large ML libraries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher compression: unzipped limit still applies.
• Five layers: 250 MB total unzipped limit.
• Ephemeral storage: /tmp, not package size.

Key takeaway: large dependencies → container images.

stem: Developers need to search X-Ray traces for requests from a specific customerId to troubleshoot complaints. What should they add to their instrumentation?

choices.text: Add customerId as an X-Ray annotation.
Log customerId to stdout only.
Add customerId as X-Ray metadata on each segment.
Put customerId in the segment name.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Adding customerId as an X-Ray annotation indexes it, so traces can be filtered by that value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• stdout only: not in traces.
• Metadata: not searchable.
• Segment name: misuse.

Key takeaway: searchable traces → annotations.

stem: During a marketing event, a critical order-processing Lambda function is throttled because a batch-reporting function in the same account consumed most of the account's concurrency. How can the developer guarantee capacity for the critical function?

choices.text: Increase the order function's memory.
Enable provisioned concurrency on the reporting function.
Set a longer timeout on the order function.
Reserved concurrency on the order function.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reserved concurrency on the order function guarantees it capacity that other functions can't consume.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More memory: doesn't reserve capacity.
• Provisioned concurrency on reporting: doesn't protect orders.
• Longer timeout: unrelated.

Key takeaway: protect critical functions → reserved concurrency.

stem: A CPU-bound Lambda function processing images runs for 8 seconds at 512 MB. The team suspects more memory would reduce both duration and cost but wants data rather than guesses. What should it do?

choices.text: Enable X-Ray active tracing to set memory automatically.
Run Lambda Power Tuning across memory settings.
Always choose the minimum memory, since cost depends only on memory.
Increase the timeout to 15 minutes.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda Power Tuning measures duration and cost across memory sizes. CPU-bound functions often get cheaper with more memory.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray sets memory: no.
• Minimum memory always cheapest: false.
• 15-minute timeout: unrelated.

Key takeaway: test memory settings empirically.

stem: An application uses lazy loading with ElastiCache. After product prices change in the database, users see old prices for up to an hour. The team wants cached prices updated when they change while keeping the cache from growing with unused keys. Which strategy fits BEST?

choices.text: Lazy loading only, with no TTL on cached items.
Disable the cache for prices entirely.
Write-through on updates plus a TTL.
Increase the cache node size.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Write-through updates the cache when prices change, and a TTL limits staleness for anything missed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No TTL: stale forever.
• Disable caching: loses performance.
• Bigger node: doesn't fix staleness.

Key takeaway: freshness → write-through + TTL.

stem: After a release, a Lambda function logs thousands of JSON error events. The developer wants the top 5 error codes over the last hour with counts, directly from the logs. What should they use?

choices.text: An S3 export of the logs and a local script.
AWS CloudTrail event history for the function.
A Logs Insights stats query by errorCode.
The Lambda console's Monitor tab.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Logs Insights query with stats count(*) by errorCode, sorted, finds the most frequent errors quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 export and script: slow.
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• Monitor tab: no grouping by error code.

Key takeaway: aggregate log errors → Logs Insights stats.
